## 1. Introduction

Phosphorus (P) is indispensable for food production and ecosystem functioning, yet its management remains predominantly linear: phosphate rock is mined, processed into fertilizers, applied to land, and ultimately dispersed through losses to waters or immobilized in residual streams. This linearity is increasingly problematic because it couples a finite, geographically concentrated resource with persistent environmental impacts, most notably eutrophication driven by excessive nutrient discharge [[1](#B1-biomass-06-00032),[2](#B2-biomass-06-00032),[3](#B3-biomass-06-00032),[4](#B4-biomass-06-00032),[5](#B5-biomass-06-00032)]. In parallel, the growing recognition of critical raw material vulnerabilities has strengthened the case for P recycling as a strategic element of long-term food security and resource governance [[6](#B6-biomass-06-00032),[7](#B7-biomass-06-00032),[8](#B8-biomass-06-00032)].

Municipal and industrial wastewaters represent a continuous, locally available secondary phosphorus stream. However, conventional phosphorus removal in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) has historically been optimized for compliance rather than recovery. Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) and chemical precipitation can achieve low effluent phosphorus concentrations; however, in many systems, phosphorus is largely transferred into sludge-bound forms, where downstream reuse is constrained by variable composition, contaminants, and the costs of further processing [[9](#B9-biomass-06-00032),[10](#B10-biomass-06-00032),[11](#B11-biomass-06-00032),[12](#B12-biomass-06-00032)]. These limitations have supported a broader shift in the field—from treatment-centric WWTPs toward water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs)—where nutrients, energy, and water are recovered as products and services rather than managed as waste [[13](#B13-biomass-06-00032),[14](#B14-biomass-06-00032),[15](#B15-biomass-06-00032),[16](#B16-biomass-06-00032)]. Framed within circular economy thinking, nutrient recovery is increasingly regarded as a core mechanism for closing material loops and reducing primary resource demand [[17](#B17-biomass-06-00032),[18](#B18-biomass-06-00032)]. In this context, the transition from linear to circular phosphorus management is closely linked to the transformation of WWTPs into WRRFs and to the development of nutrient recovery pathways ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_biomass-06-00032-f001)).

![Biomass 06 00032 g001](/biomass/biomass-06-00032/article_deploy/html/images/biomass-06-00032-g001-550.jpg "Biomass 06 00032 g001")

**Figure 1.**
Transition from a linear to a circular phosphorus economy (original schematic illustration prepared by the author).

Among phosphorus recovery routes, struvite crystallization (MgNH4PO4·6H2O) is widely regarded as one of the most mature and implementable technologies. Struvite recovery converts dissolved phosphorus into a concentrated, transportable solid; it can mitigate uncontrolled scaling in pipelines and dewatering equipment; and it yields a slow-release fertilizer containing both phosphorus and nitrogen [[19](#B19-biomass-06-00032),[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[21](#B21-biomass-06-00032)]. Full-scale experience and commercial deployment have demonstrated that struvite recovery performs most robustly in high-strength sidestreams, such as digester supernatant and dewatering centrate/filtrate, where supersaturation potential and process controllability are more favorable than in the mainstream [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[24](#B24-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032),[26](#B26-biomass-06-00032),[27](#B27-biomass-06-00032)].

Despite its technological maturity, the broader adoption of struvite recovery is still shaped by wastewater matrix effects and system-level constraints. Key practical issues include competition with calcium phosphate formation, sensitivity to organic matter and ionic strength, magnesium sourcing and cost, and the need to ensure consistent product purity and safety for agricultural use [[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[28](#B28-biomass-06-00032),[29](#B29-biomass-06-00032),[30](#B30-biomass-06-00032)]. These considerations have become more prominent as research has moved toward intensified and hybrid concepts, including electrochemical magnesium dosing and innovative process integration for nutrient recovery from complex industrial streams [[31](#B31-biomass-06-00032),[32](#B32-biomass-06-00032),[33](#B33-biomass-06-00032)]. In parallel, attention has expanded to alternative phosphorus products and routes—particularly recovery from sewage sludge ash (SSA)—which can contribute to phosphorus circularity but differ substantially from struvite in reaction pathway, product characteristics, infrastructure requirements, and deployment context [[34](#B34-biomass-06-00032),[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032)].

Regulatory frameworks increasingly influence technology selection and the marketability of recovered products. In the European Union, Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 has provided a pathway for placing recovered fertilizers on the market under defined quality and safety criteria, including categories relevant to precipitated phosphate salts and related recovered materials [[36](#B36-biomass-06-00032),[37](#B37-biomass-06-00032),[38](#B38-biomass-06-00032)]. This regulatory evolution—together with life-cycle and techno-economic evidence—has shifted the discussion from the technical feasibility of phosphorus recovery toward the identification of routes that can deliver robust environmental and economic value under real plant conditions [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[39](#B39-biomass-06-00032),[40](#B40-biomass-06-00032),[41](#B41-biomass-06-00032)]. Comparative LCA studies further indicate that such conclusions remain sensitive to system boundaries and fertilizer substitution assumptions [[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032),[42](#B42-biomass-06-00032)].

This review synthesizes recent advances in phosphorus recovery from wastewater, with a primary focus on struvite crystallization, while positioning it against conventional, competing, and complementary recovery pathways. Specifically, it (i) summarizes the physicochemical basis of struvite formation and the operational parameters governing nucleation, crystal growth, and recovery performance; (ii) compares reactor configurations, process control strategies, and commercial implementations, with emphasis on full-scale applicability; (iii) discusses product quality, environmental safety, and agronomic evidence relevant to fertilizer use; and (iv) integrates economic, life-cycle, and regulatory considerations that influence technology selection and deployment [[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[24](#B24-biomass-06-00032),[27](#B27-biomass-06-00032),[36](#B36-biomass-06-00032),[40](#B40-biomass-06-00032)]. By linking process engineering with product acceptance, practical implementation, and policy context, this review aims to support the informed selection and further development of phosphorus recovery strategies aligned with circular economy objectives.

In contrast to broader reviews that address phosphorus recovery in general or focus primarily on individual treatment routes, the present review places struvite crystallization at the center of the analysis within a single WRRF-oriented framework. Its novelty lies in integrating process fundamentals, reactor technologies, implementation evidence, product quality, environmental and economic performance, and regulatory context in order to clarify the practical conditions under which struvite recovery can be considered a robust and scalable strategy for circular phosphorus management.

### 1.1. Review Scope and Approach

This review is a critical narrative review centered on struvite crystallization as the principal phosphorus recovery route examined in the context of circular wastewater management. Other recovery pathways, including enhanced biological phosphorus removal, chemical precipitation, electrochemical systems, and sewage sludge ash recovery, are included to position struvite against conventional, competing, or complementary approaches and to clarify its practical advantages and limitations. Particular attention is given to reaction principles, process control, reactor configurations, operational constraints, product quality, and full-scale applicability. Recent literature and practically relevant studies are also emphasized to support researchers, engineers, and decision-makers involved in phosphorus recovery and WRRF design.

In this review, the term removal is used for processes that reduce phosphorus concentrations in wastewater without necessarily generating a reusable product, whereas recovery refers to processes that convert phosphorus into a form with potential for reuse, including fertilizer-grade materials such as struvite.

### 1.2. Literature Search and Review Approach

This manuscript was prepared as a critical narrative review focused on phosphorus recovery from wastewater, with primary emphasis on struvite crystallization and its position relative to competing and complementary recovery pathways. The literature survey was conducted using major scientific databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Particular emphasis was placed on peer-reviewed publications addressing phosphorus occurrence in wastewater, conventional phosphorus removal, struvite chemistry and crystallization, reactor technologies, full-scale and commercial applications, product quality, environmental and economic assessment, and regulatory aspects.

Priority was given to recent literature, especially studies published from 2020 onward, while earlier landmark publications were retained where necessary to provide the conceptual, mechanistic, or technological foundations of the field. Studies were selected and grouped according to their relevance to the main review themes, including phosphorus forms in wastewater, conventional removal versus recovery pathways, struvite formation mechanisms, operational parameters, reactor configurations, product quality, environmental and economic performance, and implementation challenges. Conference abstracts, non-substantiated claims, and sources lacking clear methodological or technical relevance were not prioritized in the comparative discussion.

## 2. Phosphorus in Wastewater: Sources, Forms, and Environmental Impact

Phosphorus enters wastewater systems from a wide range of anthropogenic and natural sources, primarily through human activities, agricultural practices, and industrial processes. These sources include municipal wastewater, industrial effluents, agro-industrial wastewater, and sludge liquor generated during wastewater treatment. Municipal wastewater is one of the most significant contributors to phosphorus pollution, as phosphorus originates from human excreta, food residues, detergents, and household cleaning products [[43](#B43-biomass-06-00032),[44](#B44-biomass-06-00032)]. Agricultural runoff also represents a major pathway, particularly in regions with intensive fertilizer use and livestock production, where phosphorus is transported from soils to surface waters and eventually enters wastewater treatment systems [[2](#B2-biomass-06-00032),[45](#B45-biomass-06-00032)]. In addition, industrial wastewater from food processing, dairy production, fertilizer manufacturing, and chemical industries can contain elevated phosphorus concentrations, depending on the process conditions and raw material composition [[10](#B10-biomass-06-00032)].

The concentration of phosphorus in wastewater varies depending on its origin and treatment stage. Typical total phosphorus concentrations in municipal wastewater range from 4 mg/L to 15 mg/L, whereas agricultural and industrial wastewater streams may contain significantly higher concentrations [[44](#B44-biomass-06-00032)]. The highest phosphorus concentrations are typically observed in sidestream flows, such as sludge dewatering liquors and anaerobic digestion effluents, which are the most suitable targets for phosphorus recovery technologies because they combine elevated phosphate concentrations with comparatively low flow rates and more favorable conditions for process control. Wastewater treatment processes often concentrate phosphorus in sludge streams, digestate, and centrate following anaerobic digestion, where phosphorus concentrations may exceed 100 mg/L, making these streams particularly suitable for recovery [[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032)].

In wastewater systems, phosphorus exists in several chemical forms, including dissolved inorganic phosphorus, organic phosphorus, and particulate-bound phosphorus. Orthophosphate (o-PO43−) is the most abundant, reactive, and readily recoverable form of phosphorus, because it directly participates in biological uptake, chemical precipitation, and crystallization reactions, including struvite formation. Organic phosphorus compounds originate from biological materials, such as cellular components and metabolic byproducts, and require enzymatic or microbial degradation before they become available for recovery or removal [[43](#B43-biomass-06-00032),[46](#B46-biomass-06-00032)]. Particulate phosphorus is typically associated with suspended solids and biomass and may be released in soluble forms during sludge treatment and digestion [[14](#B14-biomass-06-00032)].

The presence of phosphorus in wastewater has significant environmental implications. When discharged into natural water bodies without adequate treatment, phosphorus acts as a limiting nutrient for algal growth and can accelerate eutrophication, leading to excessive algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and degradation of aquatic ecosystems [[4](#B4-biomass-06-00032)]. Eutrophication negatively affects biodiversity, drinking water quality, and recreational water use and can result in increased water treatment costs and ecosystem instability [[3](#B3-biomass-06-00032)]. Consequently, strict regulations have been implemented in many countries to limit phosphorus discharge from wastewater treatment plants.

Wastewater is a valuable secondary source of phosphorus that can be recovered and reused, thereby reducing reliance on finite phosphate rock resources. The recovery of phosphorus from wastewater contributes to resource conservation, environmental protection, and circular economy implementation by converting waste streams into valuable products [[6](#B6-biomass-06-00032),[13](#B13-biomass-06-00032),[47](#B47-biomass-06-00032)]. Consequently, wastewater treatment plants are increasingly being transformed into water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs), where phosphorus recovery is integrated into the treatment processes to promote resource efficiency and environmental sustainability. From a recovery perspective, the most important distinction is between phosphorus that remains dispersed in mainstream flows and phosphorus that becomes concentrated in sludge-line sidestreams, where direct recovery is more feasible [[27](#B27-biomass-06-00032),[48](#B48-biomass-06-00032)].

The main phosphorus pathways and recovery opportunities within wastewater treatment plants are illustrated in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomass-06-00032-f002), which highlights the key streams suitable for phosphorus recovery, particularly sludge liquors, digestate, and centrate. Significant phosphorus concentrations are typically found in digested sludge and waste streams, which are key for recovery technologies such as struvite crystallization.

![Biomass 06 00032 g002](/biomass/biomass-06-00032/article_deploy/html/images/biomass-06-00032-g002-550.jpg "Biomass 06 00032 g002")

**Figure 2.**
Integration of phosphorus recovery technologies within wastewater treatment plants: From influent sources to high-value recycled products (original schematic illustration prepared by the author).

To provide a concise overview of where phosphorus is concentrated within wastewater treatment systems, [Table 1](#table_body_display_biomass-06-00032-t001) summarizes major WWTP/WRRF process streams, reporting indicative phosphorus concentration ranges, dominant phosphorus forms, and associated recovery potential. The table distinguishes between indirect recovery (phosphorus primarily retained in solids and requiring downstream processing) and direct recovery from P-rich sidestream liquors (e.g., centrate/filtrate or digester supernatant), which typically offer the most favorable conditions for crystallization-based routes such as struvite formation.

**Table 1.**
Major phosphorus-containing streams in wastewater treatment: literature-based indicative concentration ranges, dominant phosphorus forms, and recovery potential (compiled by the author from the cited literature [[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032),[26](#B26-biomass-06-00032),[27](#B27-biomass-06-00032),[28](#B28-biomass-06-00032),[49](#B49-biomass-06-00032)]).

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

As shown in [Table 1](#table_body_display_biomass-06-00032-t001), phosphorus concentrations vary markedly across WWTP/WRRF streams. The highest direct recovery potential is associated with P-rich sidestream liquors generated during digestion and dewatering, where phosphorus is predominantly present as dissolved orthophosphate. These streams offer favorable conditions for crystallization-based recovery, particularly struvite precipitation, due to elevated phosphate (and often ammonium) concentrations, comparatively smaller flow rates than the mainstream, and the greater feasibility of controlling supersaturation and product formation.

## 3. Conventional Phosphorus Removal and Recovery Technologies

Phosphorus removal from wastewater is conventionally implemented to mitigate eutrophication and protect aquatic ecosystems. Conventional wastewater treatment systems are primarily designed to reduce phosphorus concentrations in treated effluents rather than enable phosphorus recovery and reuse. In conventional wastewater treatment plants, a large fraction (often reported as ~80–95%) of the influent phosphorus is typically transferred to sewage sludge rather than recovered as a reusable product, limiting its contribution to resource circularity [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[44](#B44-biomass-06-00032),[49](#B49-biomass-06-00032)]. The two principal approaches for phosphorus removal are enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) and chemical precipitation, both of which are widely applied in municipal wastewater treatment plants worldwide [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[50](#B50-biomass-06-00032),[51](#B51-biomass-06-00032)].

Although these conventional technologies are highly effective in reducing phosphorus discharge, P transferred to sludge is rarely converted into reusable products. Increasing concerns regarding phosphorus resource depletion and environmental sustainability have driven interest in technologies that enable both phosphorus removal and recovery [[2](#B2-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032)].

### 3.1. Enhanced Biological Phosphorus Removal

Enhanced biological phosphorus removal is a widely implemented process that utilizes specialized microbial populations, known as polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (PAOs), to remove phosphorus from wastewater. These microorganisms accumulate phosphorus intracellularly as polyphosphates, allowing phosphorus removal through the separation and disposal of excess sludge [[11](#B11-biomass-06-00032),[44](#B44-biomass-06-00032)].

The EBPR process relies on alternating anaerobic and aerobic conditions. Under anaerobic conditions, PAOs release phosphorus into the liquid phase while assimilating readily biodegradable organic substrates. During the subsequent aerobic phase, PAOs uptake phosphorus in excess of their metabolic requirements and store it intracellularly, resulting in net phosphorus removal from wastewater [[11](#B11-biomass-06-00032),[52](#B52-biomass-06-00032)]. This mechanism enables phosphorus removal without routine chemical dosing, thereby reducing reagent consumption and, in some cases, operational costs.

Despite these advantages, EBPR performance is strongly influenced by operational parameters, such as temperature, pH, sludge retention time, and the availability of biodegradable carbon sources [[12](#B12-biomass-06-00032)]. Lower temperatures and insufficient readily biodegradable carbon can reduce PAO activity and favor competing populations, including glycogen-accumulating organisms (GAOs), thereby lowering phosphorus uptake efficiency. Sludge retention time and pH also influence microbial selection, phosphorus release and uptake kinetics, and the stability of biological phosphorus removal, which explains why EBPR performance can vary substantially between plants and operating regimes [[11](#B11-biomass-06-00032)]. Furthermore, phosphorus removed through EBPR is primarily stored in sludge, and subsequent sludge treatment processes, particularly anaerobic digestion, may release phosphorus back into the liquid phase. Although this release presents challenges for process stability, it also creates opportunities for phosphorus recovery from sludge liquor [[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032)]. In practice, this relationship is especially important because EBPR-enriched sludge can become a favorable precursor for sidestream struvite recovery after anaerobic digestion and dewatering. Under these conditions, phosphorus released from polyphosphate-rich biomass enters centrate or filtrate streams together with elevated ammonium concentrations, creating the high-strength sidestream environment in which struvite crystallization is most commonly implemented at full scale [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[24](#B24-biomass-06-00032)]. Thus, EBPR is not itself a struvite recovery technology, but it can indirectly support struvite formation by shifting phosphorus into sludge phases that later generate recoverable sidestream liquors.

Although EBPR is effective for phosphorus removal, phosphorus remains bound within the biomass and is not directly recovered. Recovery typically requires additional downstream processing steps, such as sludge digestion followed by struvite precipitation or chemical extraction, highlighting that EBPR alone is primarily a phosphorus removal rather than a phosphorus recovery technology [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032)].

### 3.2. Chemical Precipitation

Chemical precipitation is one of the most widely used and reliable methods for removing phosphorus from wastewater. This process involves the addition of metal salts, typically iron, aluminum, or calcium compounds, which react with dissolved phosphate ions to form insoluble precipitates that can be removed through sedimentation [[44](#B44-biomass-06-00032)].

Typical precipitation reactions are as follows:

Fe3+ + PO43− → FePO4

Al3+ + PO43− → AlPO4

Ca2+ + 2PO43− → Ca3(PO4)2

Chemical precipitation can achieve phosphorus removal efficiencies exceeding 95% under optimized conditions and is widely applied because of its operational simplicity and reliability [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032),[50](#B50-biomass-06-00032),[51](#B51-biomass-06-00032)]. Its continued widespread use is largely explained by its robustness, ease of retrofit into existing treatment trains, and predictable compliance performance under variable wastewater conditions. This process is effective under a wide range of operational conditions and is commonly used in combination with biological treatment processes.

However, in contrast to crystallization-based recovery processes, chemical precipitation produces amorphous or poorly crystalline metal phosphates with low agronomic value and limited reuse potential. Consequently, this approach is considered effective for pollution control but inefficient for phosphorus resource recovery within the circular economy framework [[49](#B49-biomass-06-00032),[53](#B53-biomass-06-00032)]. This distinction is central to the comparison with struvite crystallization. Whereas conventional Fe- or Al-based precipitation mainly immobilizes phosphorus for discharge compliance, struvite recovery aims to convert dissolved phosphorus into a concentrated and reusable fertilizer product. For this reason, chemical precipitation remains widely applied where reliable effluent control is the primary objective, while struvite crystallization is more attractive in sidestreams where recovery as a marketable product is technically and economically more feasible.

### 3.3. Phosphorus Recovery from Sewage Sludge and Sludge Ash

A substantial fraction of the phosphorus captured during wastewater treatment is transferred to sewage sludge. Consequently, sludge-derived streams constitute a key leverage point for shifting from phosphorus removal to recovery and product generation. In practice, two main recovery routes are applied: (i) recovery from sludge liquors generated during anaerobic digestion and dewatering, and (ii) recovery from sewage sludge ash (SSA) following sludge incineration [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032)].

#### 3.3.1. Recovery from Sludge Liquors

Phosphorus release during anaerobic digestion and subsequent sludge dewatering produces centrate/filtrate streams with elevated orthophosphate and ammonium concentrations, creating favorable conditions for controlled crystallization processes. These sidestream liquors are widely recognized as the most practical entry point for nutrient recovery in WRRFs because they combine high supersaturation potential with comparatively low reactor volumes and predictable hydraulic loading [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[54](#B54-biomass-06-00032)]. Struvite crystallization is particularly suited to these streams, as it enables the recovery of dissolved phosphorus in a concentrated, transportable form, while simultaneously mitigating scaling and operational fouling associated with uncontrolled precipitation [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[24](#B24-biomass-06-00032),[27](#B27-biomass-06-00032)]. This is one of the clearest practical examples of how a conventional treatment pathway and a recovery technology become linked: phosphorus initially captured in sludge during biological or chemical treatment may later reappear in digestion and dewatering liquors, where it becomes directly recoverable as struvite. In this sense, sidestream crystallization does not replace upstream phosphorus removal processes, but rather valorizes the phosphorus they transfer into sludge-derived liquid streams. Nevertheless, recovery performance remains sensitive to matrix effects such as calcium competition, organic matter, and ionic strength, which can shift precipitation toward calcium phosphates or reduce crystal quality [[30](#B30-biomass-06-00032)]. Compared with ash-based routes, recovery from sludge liquors is more directly compatible with struvite crystallization because phosphorus is already present in a dissolved and more immediately recoverable form, avoiding the additional extraction steps required for SSA processing.

#### 3.3.2. Phosphorus Recovery from Sewage Sludge Ash

For systems where sludge incineration is practiced, SSA represents an additional strategic resource recovery route [[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032),[55](#B55-biomass-06-00032)]. Incineration substantially reduces the sludge mass and volume (often by 70–90%) while concentrating phosphorus in the ash. The phosphorus content of SSA is commonly reported to be in the range of approximately 10–25% P2O5, although the exact value depends on the sludge origin and incineration conditions [[34](#B34-biomass-06-00032),[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032)]. However, phosphorus in SSA frequently occurs in mineral phases with limited solubility (e.g., various calcium phosphates and iron-associated forms), which necessitates further processing to produce plant-available or fertilizer-grade products.

Current SSA processing technologies can be grouped into wet-chemical and thermochemical routes.

* **Wet-chemical leaching.**

Wet-chemical recovery relies on acid extraction (commonly H2SO4, HCl, or H3PO4) to solubilize phosphorus, often achieving high extraction efficiencies that may exceed 90%. A critical limitation is the simultaneous dissolution of heavy metals (e.g., Cd, Pb, and Cu), which requires downstream purification steps to meet fertilizer safety criteria. Industrial concepts, such as EcoPhos, address this challenge through multistage treatment (e.g., selective precipitation and/or ion-exchange polishing) to generate higher-quality phosphate products [[34](#B34-biomass-06-00032),[54](#B54-biomass-06-00032)].

* **Thermochemical recovery.**

Thermochemical approaches treat SSA at elevated temperatures (typically 800–1000 °C), often in the presence of chloride-based additives (e.g., MgCl2 or CaCl2). These processes can volatilize or separate heavy metals while transforming phosphorus into more bioavailable mineral phases (e.g., renanite-type phases), thereby improving the agronomic usability of the product. Demonstrated examples include AshDec and Mephrec. The principal trade-off is the higher energy demand and associated operating cost compared with wet leaching, although the process can reduce liquid waste generation and simplify product handling [[34](#B34-biomass-06-00032),[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032)].

Thus, SSA recovery represents an important but technologically distinct route to phosphorus circularity: unlike struvite crystallization, it typically relies on post-incineration extraction and purification and is therefore more dependent on incineration infrastructure, chemical input, and downstream product upgrading.

Compared with sidestream struvite recovery, SSA-based routes therefore represent a less direct pathway from wastewater to reusable phosphorus products. Their practical relevance is highest in systems where mono-incineration is already established, whereas struvite crystallization is generally better aligned with WRRF configurations that seek direct sidestream recovery before phosphorus is locked into ash-derived mineral phases.

#### 3.3.3. Integrated Environmental and Economic Considerations

From a system perspective, SSA-based recovery is a classic example of technology trade-offs. Wet-chemical routes may provide high phosphorus yields but can generate chemical consumption burdens and secondary liquid residues that require management. Thermochemical routes often deliver cleaner, fertilizer-compatible solids and improved heavy-metal control, but at the expense of higher energy intensity. Recent integrated assessments emphasize that the preferred route is context-dependent and should be evaluated against local energy prices, ash quality, contaminant constraints, and the value chain for fertilizer products [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032)]. Accordingly, SSA recovery should be framed not as a universal replacement for sidestream crystallization, but as a complementary option in WRRF portfolios—particularly relevant where mono-incineration is established and policy incentives support ash-derived nutrient products.

### 3.4. Limitations of Conventional Phosphorus Removal Approaches

Although phosphorus recovery technologies have advanced markedly in the last decade, their real-world applicability is still shaped by interacting constraints that extend beyond reactor performance. Limitations arise from wastewater and sludge matrix effects, chemical demand and sourcing, process integration into existing WWTP layouts, and requirements for product quality, marketability, and regulatory compliance [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032)]. Importantly, the same plant may experience different bottlenecks depending on whether recovery is implemented in the mainstream, high-strength sidestreams (e.g., centrate/filtrate), or via sludge/ash processing routes.

In biological and chemical removal pathways, the central limitation is that phosphorus is typically transferred into sludge rather than recovered as a marketable product. EBPR performance depends on stable operational conditions and influent characteristics (e.g., availability of readily biodegradable carbon), whereas chemical precipitation is robust for compliance but increases sludge production and can reduce downstream recovery potential because phosphorus becomes bound in metal-phosphate forms [[9](#B9-biomass-06-00032),[10](#B10-biomass-06-00032),[11](#B11-biomass-06-00032),[52](#B52-biomass-06-00032)]. Consequently, additional processing steps are required to convert sludge-bound phosphorus into reusable fertilizers or industrial feedstocks [[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[54](#B54-biomass-06-00032)]. This is precisely why struvite crystallization occupies a distinct position among phosphorus management options: rather than merely transferring phosphorus into residual solids, it can recover dissolved phosphorus directly from suitable sidestream liquors as a reusable product, provided that matrix effects and process conditions remain favorable.

The limitations for struvite crystallization are more closely linked to physicochemical controls and matrix effects. Competing precipitation, particularly with calcium phosphates, can reduce the fraction of phosphate available for struvite formation and may compromise product purity and settling behavior [[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[29](#B29-biomass-06-00032)]. Chemical demand—especially magnesium dosing—and the choice of magnesium source can strongly influence operating costs and the overall environmental footprint of recovery [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[39](#B39-biomass-06-00032)]. In addition, successful long-term operation depends on reactor hydrodynamics, solids handling, and robust separation of the crystallized product; insufficient control can lead to fine formation, fouling, or unstable recovery performance [[19](#B19-biomass-06-00032),[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032)]. While sidestream applications have demonstrated reliable full-scale implementation, mainstream recovery remains more challenging because of lower phosphate concentrations and limited supersaturation [[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032)].

Sludge- and ash-based recovery routes face different constraints. Wet-chemical extraction can achieve high phosphorus dissolution; however, it often requires substantial chemical consumption and generates secondary liquid residues; additionally, the co-extraction of heavy metals necessitates purification steps to meet fertilizer safety requirements [[34](#B34-biomass-06-00032),[54](#B54-biomass-06-00032)]. Thermochemical ash treatment may improve heavy-metal control and yield more standardized products; nevertheless, it typically involves higher energy demands and dedicated infrastructure, rendering its feasibility strongly site-dependent [[34](#B34-biomass-06-00032),[35](#B35-biomass-06-00032)]. Consequently, ash-based recovery is best evaluated as part of a broader WRRF strategy that reflects local sludge management, energy context, and policy incentives rather than as a stand-alone solution.

[Table 2](#table_body_display_biomass-06-00032-t002) summarizes the main phosphorus removal and recovery pathways, including their mechanisms, indicative performances, recovery potentials, and key constraints. It should be noted that while conventional compliance-oriented chemical precipitation is generally associated with low direct recovery potential, calcium-based precipitation routes may, under selected conditions, support the formation of recoverable phosphate products such as hydroxyapatite.

**Table 2.**
Comparative overview of major phosphorus removal and recovery pathways in wastewater and sludge management (compiled by the author from the cited literature [[11](#B11-biomass-06-00032),[12](#B12-biomass-06-00032),[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[22](#B22-biomass-06-00032),[23](#B23-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032),[44](#B44-biomass-06-00032),[49](#B49-biomass-06-00032),[54](#B54-biomass-06-00032)]).

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

Overall, these limitations indicate that phosphorus recovery cannot be treated as a universal “add-on” technology. Instead, the selection and design should be guided by stream characteristics (mainstream vs. sidestream), sludge management infrastructure (digestion, dewatering, incineration), product requirements (purity and handling), and the local regulatory and market context that determines whether recovered materials can be used as fertilizers [[36](#B36-biomass-06-00032),[37](#B37-biomass-06-00032),[40](#B40-biomass-06-00032)]. This framing provides the basis for the subsequent sections, which examine the underlying chemistry and process designs—particularly for struvite crystallization—and the conditions under which recovery strategies can be translated from laboratory studies to robust full-scale practice.

### 3.5. Summary of Conventional Phosphorus Removal and Recovery Approaches

Conventional phosphorus removal strategies, most notably, EBPR and chemical precipitation, are effective for meeting discharge limits, but they remain primarily compliance-oriented because they transfer phosphorus into sludge rather than directly recover it as a reusable product [[56](#B56-biomass-06-00032)]. By contrast, sidestream struvite crystallization becomes feasible when phosphorus is present in dissolved, concentrated form in digestion and dewatering liquors, and SSA-based recovery becomes relevant mainly where incineration infrastructure already exists. Sludge- and ash-based recovery routes can achieve higher overall recovery yields; however, they typically rely on additional processing steps, chemical inputs, and/or energy-intensive infrastructure, and their feasibility is strongly site-dependent. These constraints have increased interest in crystallization-based nutrient recovery, particularly struvite crystallization, which enables the direct conversion of dissolved phosphorus into a concentrated, transportable solid with established full-scale experience. Under real plant conditions, sidestream struvite crystallization currently provides the clearest route to a concentrated and potentially marketable phosphorus product. This provides the rationale for the following section, which focuses on the fundamental principles, operating parameters, and reactor configurations governing struvite formation and recovery.

## 4. Struvite Crystallization for Phosphorus Recovery

### 4.1. Chemistry and Fundamental Principles of Struvite Formation

Struvite crystallization has emerged as one of the most effective and widely implemented technologies for phosphorus recovery from wastewater, enabling the direct conversion of dissolved phosphate into a reusable fertilizer product. Struvite, chemically known as magnesium ammonium phosphate hexahydrate (MgNH4PO4·6H2O), forms under supersaturated conditions in aqueous environments containing magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate ions and represents a thermodynamically stable mineral phase under alkaline conditions [[19](#B19-biomass-06-00032),[20](#B20-biomass-06-00032),[25](#B25-biomass-06-00032),[57](#B57-biomass-06-00032)].

Struvite formation is governed by thermodynamic and kinetic principles, particularly supersaturation, which is the driving force for nucleation and crystal growth. Struvite precipitation occurs when the ionic activity product (IAP) of magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate exceeds the solubility product constant (Ksp), resulting in thermodynamically favorable crystallization [[58](#B58-biomass-06-00032),[59](#B59-biomass-06-00032)]. The reported Ksp values for struvite range from 10−13 to 10−14; however, the apparent solubility behavior depends on factors such as temperature, ionic strength, pH, and overall solution composition, which can influence precipitation under real wastewater conditions [[60](#B60-biomass-06-00032),[61](#B61-biomass-06-00032)].

Struvite crystallization involves two main stages: nucleation and crystal growth. Nucleation refers to the formation of stable crystal nuclei from dissolved ions, which occurs when supersaturation exceeds a critical threshold. Crystal growth subsequently occurs via the incorporation of ions into the crystal lattice, resulting in the formation of larger and well-defined crystals [[58](#B58-biomass-06-00032),[62](#B62-biomass-06-00032)]. The relative dominance of nucleation versus crystal growth determines the size distribution and morphology of struvite crystals, which directly affects the recovery efficiency and downstream handling.

## Phosphorus Recovery from Wastewater in the Circular Economy: Focus on Struvite Crystallization

This is a critical narrative review published in the MDPI journal *Biomass* (2026, Volume 6, Issue 2, Article 32, DOI: 10.3390/biomass6020032) by Gergana Peeva from the Department of Chemical Technologies and Competence Center "Clean&Circle" at Burgas State University "Prof. Dr. Assen Zlatarov," Bulgaria. The article was submitted March 9, 2026, revised April 8, 2026, accepted April 10, 2026, and published April 17, 2026.

### Core Topic
The review provides a comprehensive synthesis of phosphorus recovery strategies from wastewater within a circular economy framework, with primary emphasis on struvite (MgNH4PO4·6H2O) crystallization as one of the most mature and practically implemented recovery routes. It positions struvite recovery against conventional, competing, and complementary pathways.

### Key Sections and Findings

**1. Phosphorus in Wastewater: Sources and Forms**
- Phosphorus enters wastewater from municipal (human excreta, detergents, food residues), agricultural (fertilizer use, livestock), and industrial (food processing, dairy, fertilizer manufacturing) sources.
- Typical total phosphorus concentrations in municipal wastewater range from 4 to 15 mg/L; sidestream flows (sludge dewatering liquors, anaerobic digestion effluents) can exceed 100 mg/L.
- Orthophosphate (o-PO4³⁻) is the most abundant, reactive, and recoverable phosphorus form. Phosphorus also exists as organic and particulate-bound forms.
- Phosphorus discharge causes eutrophication, algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and aquatic ecosystem degradation.

**2. Conventional Phosphorus Removal Technologies**
- **Enhanced Biological Phosphorus Removal (EBPR):** Uses polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (PAOs) under alternating anaerobic/aerobic conditions. Effective for compliance but transfers ~80–95% of influent phosphorus to sludge rather than recovering it. Performance sensitive to temperature, pH, sludge retention time, and carbon availability. EBPR can indirectly support struvite recovery by concentrating phosphorus in sludge that later releases it into sidestream liquors after digestion.
- **Chemical Precipitation:** Uses iron, aluminum, or calcium salts (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺, Ca²⁺) to form insoluble phosphates. Can exceed 95% removal efficiency but produces amorphous metal phosphates with low agronomic value and limited reuse potential.

**3. Recovery from Sewage Sludge Ash (SSA)**
- Incineration reduces sludge mass/volume by 70–90%, concentrating phosphorus in ash at ~10–25% P2O5.
- **Wet-chemical leaching** (H2SO4, HCl, H3PO4): Can achieve >90% extraction but co-dissolves heavy metals (Cd, Pb, Cu) requiring purification. Example: EcoPhos.
- **Thermochemical routes** (800–1000°C with MgCl2/CaCl2): Volatilize heavy metals and transform phosphorus into bioavailable phases (renanite-type). Examples: AshDec, Mephrec. Higher energy demand but cleaner products.

**4. Struvite Crystallization (MgNH4PO4·6H2O)**
- Formation driven by supersaturation; ionic activity product (IAP) must exceed solubility product constant (Ksp), with reported Ksp values ranging from 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁴.
- Two stages: nucleation and crystal growth, with the relative dominance determining crystal size distribution and morphology.
- Produces a slow-release fertilizer containing phosphorus, nitrogen, and magnesium; mitigates uncontrolled scaling in pipelines and dewatering equipment.
- Most robust performance occurs in high-strength sidestreams (digester supernatant, dewatering centrate/filtrate), where supersaturation potential and process controllability are favorable.
- Key challenges include: magnesium supply and cost, competition with calcium phosphate formation, sensitivity to organic matter and ionic strength, wastewater matrix effects, and mainstream application feasibility.

**5. Regulatory Context**
- EU Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 provides a pathway for placing recovered fertilizers on the market under defined quality and safety criteria, including precipitated phosphate salts and related recovered materials.

**6. Conclusions**
- Controlled sidestream struvite crystallization offers the most favorable balance between recovery efficiency, operational reliability, and fertilizer product quality under suitable plant conditions.
- Recovery technology selection must be guided by stream characteristics (mainstream vs. sidestream), sludge management infrastructure, product requirements, and local regulatory/market context.
- SSA recovery is a complementary rather than universal replacement option, most relevant where mono-incineration is established.
- The novelty of this review lies in integrating process fundamentals, reactor technologies, implementation evidence, product quality, environmental/economic performance, and regulatory context within a single WRRF-oriented framework.

### Keywords
struvite; phosphorus recovery; wastewater treatment; circular economy; nutrient recovery; bio-based fertilizers; resource recovery

Bluefield Research announced on June 6, 2025, from Boston, Massachusetts, that smart water metering has become a US$6.8 billion global market and a cornerstone of utility digital transformation. Advanced equipment including automatic meter reading and advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) enables utilities to optimize workforces, recover lost revenue, enhance customer engagement, and manage underground assets.

New service-based business models like network-as-a-service (NaaS) and metering-as-a-service (MaaS) are broadening market access for smaller or budget-constrained utilities by reducing up-front capital investments. Energy Recovery, Inc. is a global leader in energy efficiency technology, designing and manufacturing solutions for improved energy efficiency in commercial and industrial processes. The PX has been the industry standard in seawater reverse osmosis desalination (SWRO), reducing energy use by up to 60% in SWRO facilities with peak pressure recycling efficiencies up to 98%. The PX has helped SWRO supplant thermal desalination as the technology of choice.

- Emerging Technologies: CO2-based refrigeration (PX G1300) leverages the pressure exchanger platform. HFC refrigerants are being phased down globally via the Kigali Amendment (85% reduction by 2036 in developed nations), and CO2 refrigeration is a climate-friendly alternative.

This deep-dive investment analysis (published January 6, 2026) examines Badger Meter (BMI), a 1905-founded Milwaukee company that is a leading provider of smart water infrastructure technology. The article analyzes the US water utility market, Badger Meter's business model, growth prospects, competitive moat, profitability, dividends, balance sheet, and valuation.

**Market Context:** The US water market faces aging infrastructure (average pipe age ~45 years, some 75+ years old), with ~19.5% of treated drinking water lost (~$6.4 billion annually). The EPA estimates $625 billion in drinking water investments needed by 2041, plus ~$600 billion for wastewater. Currently ~40% of US water meters use AMI technology, with ~85% of demand tied to replacement cycles rather than new construction.

**Business Model:** Badger Meter generates ~90% of revenue in the US market, split between Utility Water (~88% of revenue) and Flow Instrumentation (~12%). The company sells integrated AMI solutions centered on ORION (connectivity layer) and BEACON (cloud-based SaaS software), grouped under the BlueEdge brand since 2024. Recurring revenue (SaaS, network services) currently ~7% of total revenue but growing at 28%. CEO Kenneth C. Bockhorst has led since 2019. Notable acquisition: SmartCover (January 2025), expanding into sewer/pump station monitoring with ~50% US market share.

**Growth:** Badger Meter has compounded at ~20% per year over the past decade, with 10-year revenue CAGR of ~9% and earnings CAGR of ~17%. 2024 saw revenue growth of 18% and EPS growth of 35% (boosted by post-pandemic catch-up). Q3 2025 showed ~14% revenue growth (8% organic, 6% from SmartCover). Author projects ~8-9% organic growth, ~1% acquisition contribution, and 1-2% annual margin expansion, implying ~11-13% earnings growth.

**Competitive Moat:** The author argues BMI has a genuine but not absolute moat, built on: integrated hardware+software offerings (vs. smaller component-only competitors), premium positioning (not price-based competition), technical focus on measurement accuracy and data quality, long system lifecycles (10-15 years), deep integration into utility operations creating switching costs, and lock-in effects. Competitors include Xylem (Sensus), Itron, Hubbell, and Roper Technologies (Neptune). Pricing power exists but is limited by competitive tender processes.

**Profitability & Financials:** Gross margins have improved steadily due to product mix shift toward AMI and software. Operating margins benefit from scale effects in selling/admin costs. Capital expenditures are only ~1.5% of revenue (capital-light model). Dividend increased for 33 consecutive years, with ~30% payout ratio, ~0.8% current yield, and ~14-15.5% annual dividend growth. The company holds a net cash position (~$202 million cash, ~$150 million unused credit at end of Q3 2025), with ~$112 million goodwill (~18.4% of equity).

**Valuation & Conclusion:** Using a DCF model (9-10% revenue growth, 2% terminal growth, 17-19% FCF margin, 8.2% WACC), the author arrives at a fair value of ~$149 per share, with a 20% margin of safety implying an entry price of ~$120. At the current price of ~$174, the stock trades ~31% above the suggested entry level and is deemed clearly overvalued. The author concludes BMI is a high-quality business with strong fundamentals, a solid moat, and clean balance sheet, but investors should wait for a more attractive price. <summary>
This technical paper documents the Madison Metropolitan Sewerage District's (MMSD) implementation of phosphorus recovery via struvite harvesting at its Nine Springs Wastewater Treatment Plant (NSWWTP) in Wisconsin, a 50 mgd (190,000 m³/d) advanced secondary treatment facility. The project, designed by Applied Technologies, Inc. (ATI) and implemented as part of the plant's "Eleventh Addition" beginning in 2010, aimed to address severe nuisance struvite (NH4MgPO4•6H2O) scaling problems that were causing maintenance issues in anaerobic digestion and dewatering equipment.

The system uses Ostara's Pearl® 2000 fluidized bed struvite harvesting reactors, with key components including: (1) two WAS blending/P-release tanks (1,140 m³ each) that convert intracellular phosphorus from enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) biomass into ortho-phosphate; (2) two mesophilic acid digesters (1,550 m³ each) that produce volatile fatty acids to promote phosphorus release; (3) separate filtrate management systems for WAS and digested sludge thickening operations; and (4) two Pearl® 2000 struvite reactors producing Crystal Green®, a slow-release fertilizer (5% N, 12% P as P2O5, 10% Mg). Operations began in October 2013.

RESULTS: The system achieved a 16% reduction in phosphorus load contained in Class B biosolids (from 852 to 718 kg/d, or 1,879 to 1,582 lb/d), with biosolids phosphorus content dropping from 3.8% to 3.4% (a 10% reduction). Revenues from harvested struvite increased to approximately $500/day in late 2016 (up from ~$325/day in 2014-2015), though below the design projection of ~$1,130/day. Maintenance cost savings from reduced nuisance struvite formation were estimated at approximately $1.3 million present worth.

DISCREPANCIES FROM DESIGN: Actual ortho-phosphate recovery in the reactors was below 50% for most of 2014-2016 versus the 77% design target, though recovery rates improved significantly from late 2015 through 2016 (reaching over 1,500 kg struvite/d and 190 kg P/d in the second half of 2016). Exogenous magnesium chloride consumption was nearly 250% of design (376 kg Mg/d vs. ~152 kg Mg/d expected), and ferric chloride savings were much lower than projected (only a 29% reduction vs. near-total elimination expected). Ferric chloride usage had to be maintained to control hydrogen sulfide in biogas and prevent nuisance struvite in digested sludge filtrate (since CO2 injection capacity was not used due to equipment complications). The WAS P-release system successfully converted over 80% of phosphorus in TWAS filtrate to ortho-phosphate, exceeding the design assumption of only 0.1% conversion. Actual flows to the harvester were 69% of design, and ortho-P loadings were 68% of design, while ammonia-N loadings were nearly double design projections.

The paper concludes that MMSD is poised to sustain its legacy of economic and ecological stewardship as phosphorus recovery rates continue to improve toward design targets, and recommends that future efforts carefully evaluate consequences of reduced ferric chloride consumption (e.g., hydrogen sulfide impacts on biogas).
</summary>

URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-8783/6/2/32

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Phosphorus Recovery from Wastewater in the Circular Economy: Focus on Struvite Crystallization

This is a critical narrative review published in the MDPI journal *Biomass* (2026, Volume 6, Issue 2, Article 32, DOI: 10.3390/biomass6020032) by Gergana Peeva from the Department of Chemical Technologies and Competence Center "Clean&Circle" at Burgas State University "Prof. Dr. Assen Zlatarov," Bulgaria. The article was submitted March 9, 2026, revised April 8, 2026, accepted April 10, 2026, and published April 17, 2026.

### Core Topic
The review provides a comprehensive synthesis of phosphorus recovery strategies from wastewater within a circular economy framework, with primary emphasis on struvite (MgNH4PO4·6H2O) crystallization as one of the most mature and practically implemented recovery routes. It positions struvite recovery against conventional, competing, and complementary pathways.

### Key Sections and Findings

**1. Phosphorus in Wastewater: Sources and Forms**
- Phosphorus enters wastewater from municipal (human excreta, detergents, food residues), agricultural (fertilizer use, livestock), and industrial (food processing, dairy, fertilizer manufacturing) sources.
- Typical total phosphorus concentrations in municipal wastewater range from 4 to 15 mg/L; sidestream flows (sludge dewatering liquors, anaerobic digestion effluents) can exceed 100 mg/L.
- Orthophosphate (o-PO4³⁻) is the most abundant, reactive, and recoverable phosphorus form. Phosphorus also exists as organic and particulate-bound forms.
- Phosphorus discharge causes eutrophication, algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and aquatic ecosystem degradation.

**2. Conventional Phosphorus Removal Technologies**
- **Enhanced Biological Phosphorus Removal (EBPR):** Uses polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (PAOs) under alternating anaerobic/aerobic conditions. Effective for compliance but transfers ~80–95% of influent phosphorus to sludge rather than recovering it. Performance sensitive to temperature, pH, sludge retention time, and carbon availability. EBPR can indirectly support struvite recovery by concentrating phosphorus in sludge that later releases it into sidestream liquors after digestion.
- **Chemical Precipitation:** Uses iron, aluminum, or calcium salts (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺, Ca²⁺) to form insoluble phosphates. Can exceed 95% removal efficiency but produces amorphous metal phosphates with low agronomic value and limited reuse potential.

**3. Recovery from Sewage Sludge Ash (SSA)**
- Incineration reduces sludge mass/volume by 70–90%, concentrating phosphorus in ash at ~10–25% P2O5.
- **Wet-chemical leaching** (H2SO4, HCl, H3PO4): Can achieve >90% extraction but co-dissolves heavy metals (Cd, Pb, Cu) requiring purification. Example: EcoPhos.
- **Thermochemical routes** (800–1000°C with MgCl2/CaCl2): Volatilize heavy metals and transform phosphorus into bioavailable phases (renanite-type). Examples: AshDec, Mephrec. Higher energy demand but cleaner products.

**4. Struvite Crystallization (MgNH4PO4·6H2O)**
- Formation driven by supersaturation; ionic activity product (IAP) must exceed solubility product constant (Ksp), with reported Ksp values ranging from 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁴.
- Two stages: nucleation and crystal growth, with the relative dominance determining crystal size distribution and morphology.
- Produces a slow-release fertilizer containing phosphorus, nitrogen, and magnesium; mitigates uncontrolled scaling in pipelines and dewatering equipment.
- Most robust performance occurs in high-strength sidestreams (digester supernatant, dewatering centrate/filtrate), where supersaturation potential and process controllability are favorable.
- Key challenges include: magnesium supply and cost, competition with calcium phosphate formation, sensitivity to organic matter and ionic strength, wastewater matrix effects, and mainstream application feasibility.

**5. Regulatory Context**
- EU Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 provides a pathway for placing recovered fertilizers on the market under defined quality and safety criteria, including precipitated phosphate salts and related recovered materials.

**6. Conclusions**
- Controlled sidestream struvite crystallization offers the most favorable balance between recovery efficiency, operational reliability, and fertilizer product quality under suitable plant conditions.
- Recovery technology selection must be guided by stream characteristics (mainstream vs. sidestream), sludge management infrastructure, product requirements, and local regulatory/market context.
- SSA recovery is a complementary rather than universal replacement option, most relevant where mono-incineration is established.
- The novelty of this review lies in integrating process fundamentals, reactor technologies, implementation evidence, product quality, environmental/economic performance, and regulatory context within a single WRRF-oriented framework.

### Keywords
struvite; phosphorus recovery; wastewater treatment; circular economy; nutrient recovery; bio-based fertilizers; resource recovery
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: 2026年中国水务产业现状及未来发展趋势分析--手机中研网 ---
URL: https://m.chinairn.com/scfx/20260324/173304286.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from 中研普华 (ChinaIRN), a Chinese industry research consulting firm, and features a detailed analysis of China's water utilities (水务) industry titled "2026年中国水务产业现状及未来发展趋势分析" (2026 Analysis of China's Water Utilities Industry Status and Future Development Trends), published on March 24, 2026.

KEY FINDINGS ON THE WATER UTILITIES INDUSTRY:

1. **Current Status**: China's water utilities industry has entered a high-quality development stage. In 2024, total national water usage was stable at 592.8 billion cubic meters. Water use per 10,000 yuan GDP and per 10,000 yuan industrial added value dropped 17.7% and 23.6% respectively versus 2020. Agricultural irrigation water efficiency coefficient rose to 0.580, urban public water supply pipeline leakage dropped below 9%, and rural tap water penetration reached 94% in 2024 (96% target achieved by 2025).

2. **Core Drivers (2026-2030)**: Policy top-level design from the "15th Five-Year Plan" focusing on water resource intensive use, ecological protection, urban-rural water integration, and smart water management; ecological civilization construction and dual-carbon goals driving green transformation; urban-rural integration and rising living standards expanding demand.

3. **Key Pain Points**: Regional imbalances in infrastructure (rural/western areas lagging), uneven digital/smart transformation (SMEs rely on traditional operations), and incomplete market-based pricing mechanisms limiting profitability. Shortage of professional talent and reliance on imported high-end equipment.

4. **Competitive Landscape**: Characterized by "state-owned enterprises leading, diversified participation, regional segmentation." Large SOE water groups dominate core businesses (urban water supply, large sewage treatment). Competition is shifting from project contracting to comprehensive competition in operations, technology, service quality, and smart capabilities. Market concentration is steadily increasing.

5. **Future Trends (2026-2030)**: Smart water utilities will achieve industry-wide penetration using big data, IoT, AI, and digital twins; water resource recycling (reclaimed water, rainwater, seawater desalination) and green low-carbon transformation will accelerate; industry focus shifts from infrastructure construction to "construction + operations + quality improvement."

6. **Recommendations**: For operators—upgrade infrastructure, accelerate digital transformation, expand into water-saving services, recycled water utilization, and water environment governance. For investors—focus on smart water technology R&D, water-saving equipment manufacturing, recycled water utilization, rural water facilities, and water ecological governance.

The page also includes links to related industry reports on natural gas, water utilities, barite powder, coal, Russian natural gas, shale gas, and aluminum ingots, all published by 中研普华 (ChinaIRN) between March 2026.
</summary>

URL: https://bg.qianzhan.com/trends/detail/506/220113-3c324805.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from 前瞻产业研究院 (Qianzhan Industry Research Institute) provides an analysis of China's smart water services (智慧水务) industry, published on January 13, 2022. Key findings include:

**Industry Overview & Policy Evolution:** China's smart water services industry has seen policy support evolve from "developing smart water" to "developing intelligent water" and finally to "building a smart water conservancy system" from 2014 through the "14th Five-Year Plan" period, driven by growing urban populations and water management needs.

**Market Size:** Based on calculations from construction projects published by 中项网, the 2020 smart water services market size in China was approximately 12.48 billion yuan (124.8亿元). The market is projected to reach 37 billion yuan (370亿元) by 2026.

**Supply Network Data:** China's urban water supply pipeline length reached 920,100 km in 2019 with a supply coverage rate of 98.78%. In 2020, the pipeline length grew to approximately 964,100 km with a supply coverage rate of about 98.98%. The rapid expansion of the supply network has created significant management pressure, driving demand for smart water platforms.

**Wastewater Discharge:** According to the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development's "Urban Construction Statistical Yearbook," China's wastewater discharge grew steadily from 2011-2019. In 2019, total discharge was 87.3 billion tons (555 billion tons urban, 10.2 billion tons county, 21.6 billion tons village). Preliminary estimates for 2020 put total discharge at 92.6 billion tons (58.8 billion urban, 10.5 billion county, 23.3 billion village).

**Key Listed Companies:** Major listed companies in the industry include 海峡创新 (300300), 新天科技 (300259), 汉威科技 (300007), 三川智慧 (300066), 科陆电子 (002121), and 国电南瑞 (600406).

**Future Outlook:** The industry is exploring integration with artificial intelligence for human-machine interaction applications, with significant untapped market potential in areas such as water loss control. The market is expected to reach 37 billion yuan by 2026.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: 王爱杰：中国数字水务发展现状及趋势 ---
URL: https://waterlab.hit.edu.cn/2023/0712/c5105a320565/page.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the State Key Laboratory of Urban Water Resource and Environment (Harbin Institute of Technology) and reports on a lecture presented by Professor Wang Aijie (王爱杰), Deputy Director of the Key Laboratory, at the 2023 Digital Water Innovation Forum held on June 5, 2023, at the InterContinental Hotel of the Shanghai National Exhibition and Convention Center. The report is titled "Current Status and Trends of Digital Water Services Development in China" and covers the following key areas:

**Drivers for Digital Water Development:**
- Internal drivers: high-quality drinking water requirements, environmental compliance standards, urban safety and resilience, low-carbon green development, shift from experience-based management, low operational efficiency, established information systems, and growing digital awareness.
- External drivers: policy, technology, economy, and demand.
- The recently released "Digital China Overall Layout Plan" uses a "2522" framework with two major foundations, deep integration of digital technology with "Five-in-One" construction, two major capabilities, and optimizing domestic and international digital development environments.
- Data has become a key production factor; China is entering a new era of data economy combined with the real economy.
- On March 22, 2023, the UN reconvened its Water Conference after 50 years to address the global water crisis.

**Current Status of Digital Water in China:**
- A 2017-2020 survey of 194 representative water enterprises showed widespread attention and high value recognition for digital water construction.
- China's digital water construction is transitioning from automation and informatization toward smart/intelligent development.
- Water supply enterprises focus information systems on customer service (billing, WeChat public accounts, installation management); drainage enterprises focus on operational control (automation, water quality online monitoring, central control systems).
- Goals include unmanned water plant regulation, scientific pipeline network dispatch, and efficient process control.
- Half of surveyed enterprises have established independent digital management departments; leading enterprises are characterized by strong leadership attention and deep business department involvement.
- Digital management departments are transitioning toward strategic support functions, integrating IT with business applications, and emphasizing "top-leader projects."
- Government digital water procurement projects are concentrated in southeastern and central China.
- Future 5-year investment forecasts show polarized investment trends overall, particularly in central and north China regions and for smaller enterprises (under 500,000 tons); enterprises over 500,000 tons show more balanced investment.
- China's digital water research emphasizes application and practical water issues (water quality monitoring, pollution control), while Europe and the US focus more on theory and method innovation (big data model/algorithm development). China has 95 national-level research projects related to "smart + water."
- Chinese digital water algorithms focus on AI-based watershed pollution tracing and risk prediction.
- Application examples include: Simuwater integrated brain (North China Institute), AI-based carbon accounting models at Matougang wastewater plant, digital twin-enabled low-carbon wastewater operation, and pipeline integrity management.

**Digital Water Products and Cases:**
Products include smart manhole covers, smart pumps, smart valves, smart water pillars, hydraulic control equipment, and grid-based waterlogging recognition systems. Case studies include: Fuzhou water supply network digital twin system, Yingtan water supply smart demonstration project, Yancheng remote pressure control valve project, Bo'ai No. 2 wastewater treatment plant, Caoxian Chemical Industry Park smart management, Shenzhen water quality purification plant smart control, small reservoir monitoring projects, Yangtze River ecological supervision, Songhua River smart water platform, Matougang carbon accounting platform, and smart water systems by Shenzhen Water Group, Chongqing Water Group, and Beijing Enterprises Water Group.

**Development Trends and Problems:**
Three urgent needs: (1) improved cognition of digitalization at the leadership level; (2) coordinated, unified construction and industry-recognized digital water standards (avoiding fragmented "each fighting for themselves"); (3) specialized digital water talent (universities lack relevant courses). Additional problems include: difficulty integrating technology with business operations, difficulty measuring digital water benefits (projects rarely generate independent economic returns), and difficulty forming effective industrial collaboration and core technology development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"数字水务能够提高用水效率、降低管理成本、保障水质安全，使水务管理更智能化、高效化、透明化和可持续，是水务行业发展的必然趋势。" (Digital water services can improve water efficiency, reduce management costs, ensure water quality safety, and make water management smarter, more efficient, transparent, and sustainable - an inevitable trend in the water industry.)
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://pdf.dfcfw.com/pdf/H3_AP202101231453665091_1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Dongwu Securities - Smart Water (智慧水务) Industry Deep Research Report (January 2021)

**Core Investment Thesis:** The report strategically bullish (增持/overweight rating maintained) on the smart water industry, forecasting that 2021 marks the beginning of an order explosion period. Recommended companies include: **威派格 (Weipage)**, the smart water leader; **宁水集团 (Ningshui Group)**, the smart water meter leader; and **和达科技 (Heda Technology)**, which was applying for STAR Market (科创板) listing at the time.

**Market Size:** The combined market space for smart water platforms + smart water plants (prefabricated plants) + pipeline network retrofit equipment (including secondary water supply equipment and smart water meters) exceeds 300 billion RMB (千亿级别/3000亿+). Currently, industry concentration is extremely low - leading listed companies hold less than 1% market share.

**Key Industry Drivers (4 factors):**
1. **National policy requirements:** China's drinking water quality lags the US by 50 years and Japan by 100 years. China's 2017 average urban pipeline leakage rate was 14.71% (2018: 14.62%, with 8.179 billion tons lost), significantly higher than developed countries. National policies target reducing leakage to under 10% by 2020 and mandate smart water infrastructure.
2. **Technology maturation:** 5G, NB-IoT, cloud computing, and IoT provide the technical foundation. NB-IoT enables smart meters, DMA (District Metered Area) zoning, GIS, and real-time leakage monitoring.
3. **Unified construction and management (统建统管):** Provinces including Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Hebei, Shandong, Fujian, and Guangxi are adopting unified secondary water supply construction/management models, driving platform demand.
4. **Rural drinking water upgrades during the 14th Five-Year Plan:** Estimated one county-level rural drinking water upgrade costs ~50 million RMB, implying a 100-billion+ RMB market during the 14th Five-Year Plan period.

**Market Size Breakdown:**
- Smart water platform market: Projected to grow from 82.3 billion (2018) to 251.05 billion (2023E), with 2020-2023 estimates of 125.51, 159.4, 199.25, 251.05 billion RMB respectively.
- Smart water plants (prefabricated): A 3,000-ton/day plant sells for ~20 million RMB; with ~20,000 traditional water plants nationwide, market space is estimated at 100+ billion RMB.
- Pipeline network retrofit equipment (including smart meters): Estimated at 100+ billion RMB.

**Industry Landscape:** As of H1 2020, there were ~840 smart water enterprises in China (413 manufacturing, 222 IT/software). Major tech entrants include Huawei (won Shenzhen Smart Water Phase I project for 446 million RMB in Dec 2019) and Tencent Cloud (strategic partnership with Guangdong Yuehai Water).

**Company Analysis:**

**1. 宁水集团 (Ningshui Group, code 603700):** 62-year history, smart water meter industry leader. Core advantages: (1) quality/brand ("Ningbo brand" meters, national quality award); (2) NB-IoT pioneer - first NB-IoT commercial project with Shenzhen Water Group in 2017, sold 1M+ NB-IoT smart meters in 2019, co-authored industry standards with Huawei; (3) 15 technical service centers, relationships with 2,000+ water utilities, exports to 80+ countries; (4) strong R&D with a water meter research institute and post-doctoral workstation; (5) low procurement costs. 2019 revenue was 1.371 billion RMB (+33.21% YoY). Future annual market space: 15.197 billion RMB for meter replacement (10.418 billion for smart meters).

**2. 威派格 (Weipage, code 603956):** Deep layout across the entire water industry chain. Acquired Nantong Paifike (90% stake, Sep 2019) for 30 million RMB - team from Pacific Water Treatment with 27 years of experience; acquired 20% of Water Networking (LeakView DMA leakage control solutions, Mar 2020); became controlling shareholder of Sangaogufen (20.38% stake, 2020). Strategy: Phase 1 - smart water supply; Phase 2 - smart water supply & drainage; Phase 3 - full smart water. 2016-2019 revenue: 524M→593M→652M→859M RMB (+31.73% in 2019); net profit: 106M→109M→116M→120M. Gross margins ~67-72%. Released Smart Water Plant Type I (nano-ceramic flat-sheet ultrafiltration membrane, effluent turbidity <0.1 NTU) and Type II (filter brick design, 20-year maintenance-free) at Oct 2020 product launch; expects smart water plant revenue to concentrate in 2021.

**3. 和达科技 (Heda Technology):** 18 years in water industry; integrated design, software/hardware R&D, production, sales, implementation, and service provider. Serves 400+ water utilities across China; 100+ agents nationwide. Core technologies include multi-communication protocols (NB-IoT, LoRa, 2G/3G/4G), SCADA, GIS, hydraulic modeling, and sensing technologies. 2016-2019 revenue: 117M→123M→163M→235M RMB; net profit: 28M→22M→13M→31M. Was applying for STAR Market listing.

**Valuation Snapshot (as of Jan 2020):** Weipage market cap 6.4B RMB (PE 42.91x 2020E, 21.77x 2021E); Ningshui market cap 5.58B RMB (PE 18.52x 2020E, 13.73x 2021E, buy rating).

**Risks:** Macroeconomic downturn; 14th Five-Year Plan rural/urban drinking water investment below expectations; COVID-19 related construction delays.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: 上海城投水务戴毓文：上海水务数字化转型探索与实践-中国水网 ---
URL: https://www.h2o-china.com/news/326378.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from China Water Network (中国水网) published on August 2, 2021, covering a presentation by Dai Yuwen (戴毓文), an intelligent and industrial control manager at Shanghai Chengtou Water (上海城投水务), delivered at the "2021 (6th) Water Supply Summit Forum" (2021第六届供水高峰论坛).

**Company Background:** Shanghai Chengtou Water was established in 2014, is a subsidiary of Shanghai Chengtou Group, and is a large state-owned enterprise specializing in urban water infrastructure investment, construction, and operations. It has 8 core enterprises and nearly 9,000 employees. Its business scope includes raw water supply, tap water production/distribution/sales, stormwater flood control, sewage treatment, sludge treatment, water supply/drainage investment, and water environment R&D.

**Key Themes of the Presentation:**

1. **Digitalization as a National Strategy:** Digitalization has been elevated to a national strategic priority, emphasized by the 19th National Congress of the Communist Party, the 7th World Internet Conference, and China's "14th Five-Year Plan." Both President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Keqiang have stressed accelerating digital development. The State Council and SASAC issued notices on accelerating digital transformation of state-owned enterprises, and Shanghai issued its own digital transformation guidelines.

2. **Digitalization vs. Informatization:** Informatization focuses on business digitization (business process-driven), while digitalization focuses on data-driven business transformation (digital model-driven), providing analysis and decision-making tools.

3. **Shanghai Chengtou Water's "14th Five-Year Plan" Digital Layout (6 components):**
   - Hybrid cloud & industrial internet platform infrastructure
   - Business capability + data dual-center
   - Digital twin water plants (digital twin of water production)
   - Core operations management systems
   - Smart water "new services" (integrating with government platforms like 一网统管 and 一网通办)
   - Security assurance systems

4. **Huangpu Demonstration Zone Project:** Shanghai Chengtou Water broke down business and data silos for the first time, connecting the entire industrial chain from raw water to water supply. The project analyzed three elements: "water" (pipeline inspection inefficiency, lack of automatic water quality alerts, difficult leak location, high equipment maintenance costs), "plant" (manual process adjustment, manual reporting, high energy consumption, difficult chemical dosing balance), and "people" (scattered user data, poor repair timeliness, difficult debt collection, slow customer complaint handling, passive service). The project uses a microservices architecture with capability centers to integrate "N businesses, 1 platform, 1 data center."

5. **"14th Five-Year Plan" Outlook:** Five digital initiatives ("full sensing," "online," "intelligent," "data-driven," "all-channel"), 3D visualization of the entire industrial chain (digital mapping), and infrastructure resilience for millions of users (especially during extreme cold weather events like the 2016 and 2020 cold snaps). The ultimate goal is customer-centric transparent and high-quality services: digital touchpoints across all channels, unified water bills, transparent water quality information, timely repair responses, 24/7 consulting, and proactive customer care.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"水务行业数字化转型需要从思维进行转变，上海城投水务的数字化建设将传统的供水企业与互联网的思维相结合，并从需求侧出发，从'龙头'到'源头'对全产业链智慧供水赋能" (Water industry digital transformation requires a mindset change; Shanghai Chengtou Water combines traditional water supply with internet thinking, and from the demand side, empowers smart water supply across the entire industrial chain from the 'tap' to the 'source').
</key_excerpts>
