## Smart meters will be pivotal in avoiding future water deficits, enhancing customer engagement and affordability – but they’ll only be effective if supported by good governance

Speaking in 2019, Sir James Bevan, then chief executive of the Environment Agency (EA) warned that there was an “existential threat” to the UK’s “economy, environment, security, happiness, [and] way of life” due to a future anticipated water deficit caused by climate change and population growth. If no action were to be taken by 2050, Bevan warned, “the amount of water available could be reduced by 10-15 per cent, with some rivers seeing 50-80 per cent less water during the summer months”. The [latest EA projections](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-review-of-englands-draft-regional-and-water-resources-management-plans/19b2f89b-e5ad-4387-afab-884c275437ee), updated in December 2024, put a solid figure on this: without intervention, demand for water will exceed supply by 5 billion litres a day in 2050.

That [speech](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/escaping-the-jaws-of-death-ensuring-enough-water-in-2050), entitled, “Escaping the jaws of death: ensuring enough water in 2050”, is arguably the most important discourse on the UK’s water sector this century, the first time someone in such a position of authority raised the national consciousness about the possibility of running out of water.

By calling for the UK to “reduce demand and increase supply” in the face of water scarcity, Bevan was in effect arguing for greater resilience. The good news is that we know how to achieve this, with tools already at our disposal, including building reservoirs, increasing the number of cross-company connections, and having more customer metering to minimise leakage.

### Solutions: reservoirs and cross-company transfers

The six years since Bevan made that speech have seen considerable progress in this area, with reported leakage levels down 11 per cent, according to [Ofwat’s 2023-24 Water Company Performance Report](https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/WCPR-23-24.pdf).

New reservoirs are being planned and built. The [Havant Thicket Reservoir](https://www.portsmouthwater.co.uk/new-reservoir/), in Hampshire, is due to come online in 2029 and will be the first new reservoir in England for almost 40 years, supplying water to 160,000 properties. Other reservoirs are due to follow.

Cross-company transfer schemes are also being designed and developed, with maybe the most eye-catching being the [Grand Union Canal Transfer Scheme](https://guctransfer.co.uk/). Still in the consultation stages, when it eventually opens in 2032, it will move water from the midlands to the southeast, fusing infrastructure originally built 200 years ago with modern engineering.

While new reservoirs and cross-company transfers are impressive, necessary and essential, water utilities are not just relying on big supply-side infrastructure to solve the problem. They are also focused on driving down demand, nationally having committed in their draft regional and water resources management plans to [halving leakage and reducing per capita consumption to 110 litres by 2050](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-review-of-englands-draft-regional-and-water-resources-management-plans/19b2f89b-e5ad-4387-afab-884c275437ee).

To support these ambitions, water utilities in England are turning to smart water meters that can provide companies and their customers – both household and non-household (business and industrial premises) – with real time usage data.

Presently the EA estimates that 13 per cent of households and under 10 per cent of non-households have smart meters. That is about to change: between now and 2030, water utilities in England are planning to install almost 10 million smart meters. About three-quarters of these installs will be an upgrade to an existing meter, with the remainder going to previously unmetered properties.

This will result in 48 per cent of households and non-households having a smart meter by 2030, according to the EA. By 2040 it is expected that 73 per cent of household and 63 per cent of business and industrial premises will have a smart meter.

### Combatting water deficit through demand management

Two-thirds of that 5 billion litres by 2050 deficit should be combatted through demand management, according to the EA.

With conventional meters only being read twice a year, leaks are often only identified when there is a high bill. By then, of course, a great deal of water could have been lost over a period of months. This system also fails to identify small leaks that don’t have a significant impact on bills, but do add up to significant loss over time. Smart meters, by contrast, provide frequent, real time data that flags even small leaks almost immediately.

It’s for this reason that the EA has asked water utilities to stop installing conventional meters and prioritise the “rapid and essential transition” to smart meters.

In the eight years since Thames Water installed its first smart meter, the company’s fleet of now more than a million meters have identified more than [80,000 leaks](https://www.thameswater.co.uk/news/thames-water-surpasses-1-million-smart-meter-installations). This has saved 57 million litres of water a day, or enough to supply around 160,000 homes – the number projected to be served by the Havant Thicket Reservoir!

[Severn Trent](https://www.stwater.co.uk/) have also seen significant benefit in the three years since it installed the first of its 350,000 smart meters. Savings of more than [4m litres](https://www.stwater.co.uk/news/news-releases/severn-trent-customers-saving-four-million-litres-of-water-a-day/) a day are being quoted, equivalent to the volume that some of their groundwater sites produce each day.

While at Anglian Water, water going into supply in their region is now 100m litres a day lower, thanks to smart meters, according to [Doug Spencer](https://www.ciwem.org/events/smart-water-metering-unlocking-the-benefits-webinar), the company’s head of smart metering. “Smart meters have a real impact,” he says.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Over the next five years the 15 English water utilities plan to install [almost 10 million smart meters](https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/PR24-draft-determinations-Expenditure-allowances-to-upload.pdf). The number of installations varies from utility to utility due to the water stress of an area, the number of smart meters already installed and the size of the utilities.

### Smarter customer engagement through smart meters

Smart meters are great for the environment, but they are also great for encouraging interaction between water utilities and customers, with customers able to read their own meters from the convenience of a website or app. The ease of accessing meter reads, and the increased frequency of meter reads are two key reasons that the [Consumer Council for Water (CCW)](https://www.ccw.org.uk/) is supporting the smart meter roll out, according to its CEO, [Mike Keil](https://www.ccw.org.uk/staff-member/dr-mike-keil/). While Keil believes that all meters “empower” customers, he feels that this is especially true of smart meters.

Utilities are expecting smart meters to be a catalyst for an enhanced relationship with customers. By proactively alerting customers to leaks, utilities can begin “more and better conversations”, says Spencer. These conversations, along with the analytics made possible by smart meters, can lead to “sustainable reductions”, according to Dene Marshallsay, director at [Artesia](https://artesia-consulting.co.uk/), a consultancy specialising in understanding water demand.

Artesia is supporting several large utilities with their interpretation of smart meter data. By combining smart meter analytics and social science techniques, a water company can create a so-called ‘demand fingerprint’ for each customer, says Marshallsay, which can then be used to tailor its engagement with that household or business. In this way, messaging around issues like saving water is more likely to land.

Smart meters are also likely to be a spur for more creative interactions between utilities and customers. We are already seeing evidence of this, with Severn Trent leading an [Ofwat Innovation Fund](https://waterinnovation.challenges.org/winners/behavioural-incentivisation/) project to understand if incentivising customers with Nectar points can lead to consistent water saving behaviour. This could result in water utilities no longer being seen as companies whose only interaction with their customer is to send them an annual bill. Instead, they may be seen as companies that reward customers for sustainable environmental behaviours. Quite a paradigm shift!

Smart meters could also improve affordability. The way water utilities have charged their customers has changed little over the past 30 years, but over the next five years, all water utilities in England will conduct small-scale pilots looking into new ways of charging, with the aim of improving affordability and water efficiency.

The first of the trials is already underway, with [Affinity Water](https://www.affinitywater.co.uk/) having introduced what’s known as a ‘rising block tariff’ for 1,500 customers in the Stevenage region. This means that those using less water pay less per unit, while those using more, pay more per unit. The first 30,000 litres of water a year are free of charge for customers on the pilot, which Affinity is calling its [WaterSave Tariff trial](https://www.affinitywater.co.uk/billing/watersavetariff). While the trial will not be completed until late 2025, the utility predicts that two thirds of households will save money.

### Good governance

But empowering customers to use less water and save money isn’t enough by itself. Smart metering must be underpinned by good governance, including in areas like data protection. While “not a trivial thing” to put in place, says Marshallsay, once set up, it enables water utilities to “get much better value out of the data” from smart meters.

Keil warns that water utilities need to consider how they “roll out their metering in a consumer-friendly way”. He points to the CCW’s [Household Customer Complaints Report 2024](https://www.ccw.org.uk/publication/household-complaint-handling-report-2024/#:~:text=CCW%20has%20published%20its%20annual,or%20to%20a%20satisfactory%20standard.), which shows that complaints around metering 30 per cent in 2023-24, from 1,539 in 2023-24 to 1,997.

The growth of smart metering is an exciting challenge that the industry is working hard to meet. The ‘final determinations’ of Ofwat’s 2024 price review (PR24), published in December 2024, will provide water companies with [£1.7 billion to deliver almost 10 million smart meter installs](https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/PR24-final-determinations-Price-control-deliverables-appendix.pdf) over the next five years. Earlier adopters have been sharing their learning with others in the industry through sector-wide groups such as the Smart Metering Advisory Group (SMAG) and the Croydon Group (named after the location of its first meeting), both of which meet frequently to focus on improving smart metering policy and practices.

Smart meters are a transformational development in the water sector. Customers, utilities and regulators are all keen to see their expansion and a likely exponential growth in their adoption over the next five years. Together with large infrastructure, they are building greater resilience, one smart meter at a time. By doing so they will help society avoid what Sir James Bevan called “the jaws of death”.

Equally exciting is the fact that smart meters are putting customers at the heart of the solution, enabling us all to save water and help ensure that there is plenty available for future generations. Now that really is smart!

---

**Author:** Mikal Willmott, leakage performance and strategy manager at Severn Trent

# AI Water Breakthrough

Severn Trent will soon be implementing artificial intelligence and machine learning to automate waste catchments in the UK.

[Mark Watson](/14223068)

,

[Darren Duncan](/14223067)

,

[James Ballard](/14223066)

Jan. 12, 2022

6 min read

[Add Us On Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=waterworld.com)

Photo courtesy Severn Trent.

![Water companies have seen a significant increase in hydraulic sewer flooding in the last five years. Models of population growth and climate change predict that this problem will increase in the future.](https://img.waterworld.com/files/base/ebm/ww/image/2021/12/16x9/2201WWint_p01.61c24a2f6a34d.png?auto=format,compress&fit=fill&fill=blur&q=45?w=250&width=250)

Water companies have seen a significant increase in hydraulic sewer flooding in the last five years. Models of population growth and climate change predict that this problem will increase in the future.

It’s a brave and bold solution to combine artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) to optimize a sewage network, but that is what the United Kingdom’s second-largest water company, Severn Trent, is setting out to do after winning £2M ($2.6M USD) of funding from Ofwat’s Water Breakthrough Challenge.

Severn Trent, the water utility company for the UK Midlands region, has long recognized that the potential for fully autonomous waste catchments exists; they just needed the means to unlock it. Severn Trent began to collaborate with fellow utilities Hafren Dyfrdwy, South West Water, Southern Water, and Thames Water — as well as global innovators at Blackburn Starling, BT, Microsoft, Rockwell Automation, 8Power, and the University of Exeter and National Cyber Security Centre. This collaboration of organizations recently secured funding to explore how AI can enable autonomy in waste catchments in an innovation project which will run for three years.

The UK’s water industry and its regulators agree that climate change, population growth, urban expansion, increasing water consumption, and changing customer behaviors mean that the industry needs solutions that are flexible and capable of adapting to what future demand will throw at them.

Photo courtesy Severn Trent.

![Historically, the UK water sector has used a legacy of low-tech solutions in waste catchments to minimize the risk of asset failure.](https://img.waterworld.com/files/base/ebm/ww/image/2021/12/2201WWint_p02.61c24a2f68c8d.png?auto=format,compress&fit=max&q=45?w=250&width=250)

Historically, the UK water sector has used a legacy of low-tech solutions in waste catchments to minimize the risk of asset failure.

The motivation for this innovative research is geared toward improving the region’s customer experience and environmental wellbeing by reducing flooding and pollution. The UK water sector has a legacy of suboptimal, low-tech solutions in waste catchments to minimize the risk of asset failure (which can lead to sewage pollutions and flooding, impacting customers and the environment), reduce energy consumption and process emissions, and maximize resource recovery.

Water companies have seen a significant increase in hydraulic sewer flooding in the last five years (over 500 percent in some cases) and the water industry accounts for 35 percent of river pollutions. Models of population growth and climate change predict that this problem will continue to increase over the coming years.

Between 2020-2025, population growth is projected to reach 1.39 million, with an additional 371,000 people moving into Severn Trent’s service area, an increase of 12.1 percent from the 2015-2020 period. Other water companies will experience similar levels of increased pressure on their networks.

The UK’s national weather service predicts that over the next 50 years, the UK’s winters will become 30 percent wetter and summers will become 60 percent drier.

### Understanding the Problem

Progress has been made across the water industry in several aspects of pollution prevention. However, these have generally focused on standalone solutions rather than holistic solutions.

Historically, water companies have developed and deployed technologies for individual challenges, such as: intelligent sewage pumping stations that utilize controller logic to detect storm events, automatically optimizing for energy or flow; AI models to predict the likelihood and customer impact of sewage pumping station failures or floods, allowing for proactive intervention; applications for automated sluice gates to attenuate flows, optimize storage, and calm flow into treatment works; and low-cost IoT sewer sensors to warn of blockages before they affect customers.

### AI is Changing the Way the World Works

Photo courtesy Rockwell Automation.

![To date, individual water companies have made several inroads into the application of AI — but only for small performance improvements.](https://img.waterworld.com/files/base/ebm/ww/image/2021/12/2201WWint_p03.61c24a2f66dd3.png?auto=format,compress&fit=max&q=45?w=250&width=250)

To date, individual water companies have made several inroads into the application of AI — but only for small performance improvements.

The large scale population growth and climate change is affecting customers across the UK. However, AI and machine learning present a significant opportunity to bring these solutions together into a single autonomous catchment management solution, able to respond to the increasing demands on Severn Trent’s assets and customers, as well as the environment.

One of the key barriers to the adoption of AI is its vulnerability to cyber threats. Proposed AI solutions are often rejected by water companies due to a lack of confidence in the security of the system. But, with the right security in place, AI has the potential to transform the way the water sector operates.

To date, individual water companies have made inroads into the application of AI, but only for small performance improvements. To drive transformative change and realize the benefits for stakeholders, it’s imperative to share data, best practices, and innovative solutions within the sector.

Severn Trent’s cross-sector coalition proposes to pilot an autonomous waste catchment in the island’s Midlands and Southwest regions. This will combine emerging technologies for comprehensive testing, and create a shared blueprint that is tested, proven, and ready to be scaled across the UK.

With the blueprint, water companies would be able to:

* Minimize the risk of flooding and pollutions in real time through intelligent localized autonomous control of the catchment;
* Minimize the risk of asset failure by integrating prescriptive, condition-based maintenance of sewage pumping stations and rising mains;
* Reduce energy consumption and process emissions, and maximize resource recovery by maintaining steady-state conditions to the sewage treatment works; and
* Protect the system from cyber threats and malicious attacks (a key barrier to the adoption of AI solutions) by developing a security wrapper for connected Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) devices.

Over the next three years, Severn Trent and its partners will create these blueprints and integrate the appropriate sector cybersecurity requirements for the use of AI technology on a waste or water network.

### Partnership Working

Partnering with Rockwell Automation has enabled Severn Trent to leverage the company’s domain expertise gained within the Information Technology/Operational Technology (IT/OT) layer to bring about scalable solutions for all disciplines of the water industry.

Rockwell Automation is working closely with Severn Trent and their partners, providing access and collaboration with specialist teams in the areas of network and cyber security, AI, and machine learning applications — along with advice and support on other emerging technologies. Having provided unique solutions within other sectors of business, many of these technologies will be transferable to the water industry.

Rockwell Automation’s specialists will work with Severn Trent to define the best vendor-agnostic technologies and solutions; leveraging the considerable expertise gained across many different verticals to help develop a solution that delivers a real-world application.

“This application will show how the adoption of AI and machine learning, in addition to access to both real time and historical data, can deliver an intelligent Connected Enterprise application that can be scalable and deployable within the UK water sector,” Mark Watson, water and wastewater solutions provider at Rockwell Automation said.

Photo courtesy Rockwell Automation.

![Severn Trent’s cross-sector coalition would combine emerging technologies for comprehensive testing, and create a shared blueprint to be scaled across the UK.](https://img.waterworld.com/files/base/ebm/ww/image/2021/12/2201WWint_p04.61c24a2f60f67.png?auto=format,compress&fit=max&q=45?w=250&width=250)

Severn Trent’s cross-sector coalition would combine emerging technologies for comprehensive testing, and create a shared blueprint to be scaled across the UK.

In addition to access to specialist teams, Rockwell Automation is providing the software and hardware to ensure the best possible solution, in order to create a new standard for future deployment within the sector.

### Short and Long Term Benefits

The project is ambitious. In the short term, it will optimize the use of latent storage within networks, optimize the flow into sewage treatment works and develop a security wrapper for connected devices.

The longer-term outcomes will minimize the risk of asset failure, reduce energy consumption and process emissions, facilitate sustainable growth in communities and allow catchments across the UK to leapfrog the technology gap, resulting in fewer spills, floods, and pollution. **WW**

args.summary:
This article from WaterWorld magazine (January 2022) describes Severn Trent, the UK's second-largest water company, implementing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to automate waste catchments. Severn Trent won £2M ($2.6M USD) from Ofwat's Water Breakthrough Challenge to fund a three-year innovation project exploring how AI can enable autonomy in waste catchments.

The project involves collaboration with fellow utilities Hafren Dyfrdwy, South West Water, Southern Water, and Thames Water, as well as global innovators including Blackburn Starling, BT, Microsoft, Rockwell Automation, 8Power, the University of Exeter, and the National Cyber Security Centre. The motivation is to improve customer experience and environmental wellbeing by reducing flooding and pollution.

Key context: Water companies have seen a significant increase in hydraulic sewer flooding in the last five years (over 500% in some cases), and the water industry accounts for 35% of river pollutions. Between 2020-2025, population growth is projected to reach 1.39 million, with an additional 371,000 people moving into Severn Trent's service area (a 12.1% increase from 2015-2020). The UK's national weather service predicts winters will become 30% wetter and summers 60% drier over the next 50 years.

The project aims to create a shared blueprint for autonomous waste catchment management that includes: minimizing flooding and pollution risks in real time through intelligent localized autonomous control; minimizing asset failure risk through prescriptive, condition-based maintenance; reducing energy consumption and process emissions while maximizing resource recovery; and protecting systems from cyber threats by developing a security wrapper for connected Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) devices.

A key barrier to AI adoption in the water sector is vulnerability to cyber threats, which has caused water companies to reject proposed AI solutions due to lack of security confidence. Rockwell Automation is partnering to provide IT/OT domain expertise, specialist teams in network/cyber security and AI/machine learning, and software/hardware to create a new standard for future deployment. In the short term, the project will optimize latent storage within networks, optimize flow into treatment works, and develop a security wrapper for connected devices. Longer-term outcomes include reduced asset failures, lower energy consumption and emissions, and fewer spills, floods, and pollution across UK catchments.
args.key_excerpts: "This application will show how the adoption of AI and machine learning, in addition to access to both real time and historical data, can deliver an intelligent Connected Enterprise application that can be scalable and deployable within the UK water sector," Mark Watson, water and wastewater solutions provider at Rockwell Automation said.

# Thames Water signs AI satellite deal to plug 100 million litres of daily leaks

![Olivia Tempest](https://wp.smartwatermagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/redactor-olivia-tempest.jpg)

Written by[Olivia Tempest](/blogs/olivia-tempest)

2 min read

[Follow us on Google Discover](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqNAgKIi5DQklTSEFnTWFoZ0tGbk50WVhKMGQyRjBaWEp0WVdkaGVtbHVaUzVqYjIwb0FBUAE?hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US:en)

Thames Water has **signed a 13-month contract** with the North East-based start-up **Origin Tech** to deploy AI-driven satellite technology across its network, in a partnership the companies say could cut water losses by more than 100 million litres a day.

The agreement makes Thames Water the first water company in Britain to fully integrate Origin Tech's Origin Orbit® system into its day-to-day leakage operations. The technology uses satellite data and artificial intelligence to pinpoint potential underground leaks within a 30-metre search radius, a method the firms argue is faster and more accurate than traditional detection.

A team of 20 specialists will be deployed under the contract, with each crew expected to **identify 25 leaks a week.**

The deal follows an 18-week trial during which Origin Orbit® located more than 800 leaks across Thames Water's network. The trial saved an estimated 8.7m litres of water a day, enough, the company said, to fill more than three Olympic-sized swimming pools. Some of the leaks identified were running at more than 10 litres per second, equivalent to filling a bath every eight seconds.

> The technology uses satellite data and artificial intelligence to pinpoint potential underground leaks within a 30-metre search radius

Shane Gloster, head of leakage at Thames Water, said: "A huge proportion of our leaks are never seen by customers, as they are underground and hard to find. To repair these as quickly as we can, it is vital that we use the latest innovative technology available. Partnering with Origin Tech, deploying their satellite data to detect leaks gives us a faster and more accurate indication of where the network has issues, enabling us to work more efficiently in our pursuit of bringing down water loss."

Founded in 2019, Origin Tech now works with **12 UK water companies** and says its technology has helped prevent more than three billion litres of water being lost through leakage. According to the firm, 92% of the leaks identified through Origin Orbit® are non-visible.

John Marsden, co-founder of Origin Tech, said: "With one-fifth of all water in the UK being lost through leakage every year, the need for innovative solutions is evident. It is great to see that water companies like Thames Water are embracing innovations that will make a difference. We are very proud to be working with them towards a collective goal of reducing water waste and supporting more sustainable operations."

# Almost 600,000 smart water meters installed in the Midlands

![Smart meter installation ](https://www.watermagazine.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/severn-trent-smart-1.jpg)

### **Severn Trent has installed almost 600,000 smart meters for customers – helping people to track their water usage and potentially save money.**

The region-wide rollout of the free meters began in 2021 and anyone interested can sign up by visiting the company website.

Seven Trent has been encouraging customers to think about their water usage, with smart meters making it easier to see how much they’re using, each day.

The meters also help the company help identify leaks quicker so they can inform households of any issues – potentially saving hundreds of litres of water.

**Stuart Leach, Smart Metering Operations Lead at Severn Trent, said:**

“Leaks can cost people a lot of money, whether that is on bills or damage caused to properties.

“Many people aren’t aware they’re responsible for fixing any broken pipes on their property. If you have a smart meter, we can alert you to any potential leaks and let you know so you can get them fixed quickly.

“We offer plenty of advice about this, including how to find an approved plumber on our website.”

Severn Trent’s smart meter programme forms part of wider plans to help customers reduce water consumption, with predictions estimating some UK regions could be facing some form of water scarcity by 2035.

This is the official website of 图观 (Tuguan), a digital twin (数字孪生) platform by 数字冰雹, specifically featuring its "智慧水务数字孪生 IOC" (Smart Water Digital Twin IOC) system solution page.

**Company/Platform Overview:**
- 图观™ (Tuguan) is a digital twin platform that provides end-to-end scene construction, zero-code development, and low-code development tools
- Core products include: 图观模型编辑器 (model editor), 场景编辑器 (scene editor), 场景服务器 (scene server), 城市生成器 (city generator), streaming scene tools (场景编辑器/打包服务器/场景服务器/场景生成器), 应用编辑器 (application editor), 应用服务器 (application server), 统一开发API (unified development API), and API调试器 (API debugger)
- The platform uses self-developed 3D rendering engines (not repackaged foreign commercial engines) with dual rendering kernel support: WebGL architecture and Web Streaming architecture

**Smart Water Digital Twin IOC System:**
The system integrates data resources from water regulatory departments' existing information systems, combining 5G, big data, cloud computing, AI, and converged communications. It covers multiple business domains:
- 水环境监测 (Water environment monitoring)
- 城市供水监测 (Urban water supply monitoring)
- 排水运营监测 (Drainage operations monitoring)
- 水生态监测 (Water ecology monitoring)
- 水工程监测 (Water engineering monitoring)
- 水安全监测 (Water safety monitoring)

**Key Functional Capabilities:**
1. **业务决策赋能 (Business decision enablement):** Real-time monitoring of water sources, pipe networks, pollutant discharge enterprises; water resource monitoring (rivers, lakes, reservoirs, groundwater); urban water use monitoring via rasterization; water supply pipe network monitoring; plant/station operations monitoring (sewage plants, drainage pumping stations); drainage network monitoring; key pollutant discharge enterprise monitoring with data threshold alerting; "river-lake profiles" (河湖画像) for ecological monitoring; water safety monitoring including river water levels, flow, precipitation trends with threshold-based alerts for flood prevention

2. **数字孪生赋能 (Digital twin enablement):** Full-element scene object integration (vector geographic data, building models, city facilities); multi-source data fusion (databases, cloud platforms, IoT, video surveillance, converged communications); multi-type map data support (administrative maps, terrain, satellite maps, PGIS, Tianditu, high-precision elevation, oblique photography, drone aerial, BIM); full-scale 3D twin rendering with film-grade visual effects; full-element object interactive control (map-chart linkage, layer filtering, target profiling)

3. **智能运维赋能 (Intelligent operations enablement):** Complete closed-loop business workflow of "智能预警-智能感知-智能处置-智能考评-智能改进" (intelligent early warning - intelligent sensing - intelligent disposal - intelligent assessment - intelligent improvement), including time/space/data dimension threshold alert rules, integration of 12345/122/AI/IOT platforms, converged command platform for automatic dispatch, and quantitative assessment systems

4. **基础平台赋能 (Foundation platform enablement):** Converged communications (video conferencing, handheld radios, teleconferencing); AI recognition; video surveillance integration (Hikvision, Dahua, Huawei platforms, AI/AR/eagle-eye/high-point/PTZ/IVS systems); business system integration across departments; IoT sensing aggregation; multi-screen integrated linkage (large/medium/small screens with synchronized data display)

**Product Advantages:**
- 效果非凡 (Outstanding visual effects): Photographic detail, full-scale rendering from solar system to individual screw detail, film-grade real-time rendering
- 全工具链交付 (Full toolchain delivery): One-stop development toolchain covering 3D scene construction, scene service debugging, and twin application development
- 功能强大 (Powerful functionality): Serves as decision center, early warning center, governance center, command center, and display center
- 跨平台支持 (Cross-platform support): Dual rendering kernels, private cloud or public cloud deployment options
- 自主可控 (Self-controlled/independent): Self-developed core rendering engine, not subject to foreign technology constraints, supports deep customization
- 良好口碑 (Good reputation): Self-owned technical team providing full-service support from design to delivery

**Industry Solutions Offered:**
The platform serves multiple industries: smart city, public safety (police, traffic management, prison, emergency response, meteorology, cybersecurity), agriculture/water management, smart transportation (traffic, airport, harbor, highway, subway, bus), smart parks (campus, scenic areas, hospital), industrial manufacturing (factory, warehousing, coal mine, electricity), smart data centers, aerospace/military, and marketing display (product display, data visualization screens). Success cases are provided for each sector.

**Contact/Support:**
- Hotline: 400-689-6796

<summary>
This webpage from pestel-analysis.com provides a comprehensive analysis of Xylem Company's competitive landscape. Xylem is a water technology company with approximately $8.6 billion in 2024 revenue, about 23,000 employees, and reach in 150+ countries. The company, which dates to a 2011 ITT spin-off and closed a $7.5 billion Evoqua acquisition in 2023, competes primarily in water infrastructure, treatment, and smart monitoring for utilities, industry, and buildings.

KEY COMPETITORS: Veolia is the toughest overall challenger, with 2024 revenue of about €44.7 billion and the ability to bundle water, waste, and energy services (strengthened by its 2022 Suez merger). Pentair and Grundfos compete in pumps and energy-efficient applications. Badger Meter is a strong rival in smart metering and utility analytics (2024 revenue about US$827 million). Sulzer, Franklin Electric, Watts Water, and local OEMs compete on price, product fit, and delivery speed.

COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGES: Xylem's competitive edge rests on its installed base (creating switching costs for utilities), deep service relationships, engineering credibility, and a broad portfolio spanning transport, treatment, measurement, and resource recovery. Core brands include Flygt, Goulds Water Technology, Sensus, and YSI. The Evoqua deal broadened treatment coverage and recurring service capabilities.

MARKET TRENDS: Key industry drivers include aging infrastructure (ASCE gave US drinking water infrastructure a D grade in 2025), PFAS compliance spending (US EPA set first national drinking water limits for PFAS in April 2024), water scarcity, digital leak detection demand, and the shift toward recurring software/service revenue. Xylem is strongest in North America and Europe, with price-sensitive emerging markets giving local rivals more room.

OUTLOOK: The competitive outlook appears stronger but not risk-free. Scale helps but execution discipline matters more; municipal budget pressure, integration risk, and price competition can compress margins. The company's strategic positioning relies on recurring service, engineering depth, and cross-selling across segments, with growth expected to hold firm through 2025-2026.
</summary>

This is the Form 10-K Annual Report for fiscal year 2023 filed by Energy Recovery, Inc. (ERII) with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, covering the year ended December 31, 2023. - As of February 15, 2024, there were 57,078,540 shares of common stock outstanding.
- The company is classified as a large accelerated filer.

BUSINESS OVERVIEW:
Energy Recovery, Inc. is a global leader in energy efficiency technology, designing and manufacturing solutions for improved energy efficiency in commercial and industrial processes. The company has been incorporated in Delaware since 2001, with corporate headquarters, principal R&D, and manufacturing in San Leandro, California, additional manufacturing/warehouse space in Tracy, California, and offices/warehouse in Katy, Texas. The company maintains a global direct sales team servicing the U.S., Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and Asia.

CORE TECHNOLOGY:
The company's flagship technology is the PX® Pressure Exchanger® (PX), an isobaric energy recovery device that transfers pressure energy between high- and low-pressure liquid/gas streams through continuously rotating ducts with micron-level clearances. The PX has been the industry standard in seawater reverse osmosis desalination (SWRO), reducing energy use by up to 60% in SWRO facilities with peak pressure recycling efficiencies up to 98%. The PX has helped SWRO supplant thermal desalination as the technology of choice.

MARKETS AND PRODUCTS:
- Desalination (primary market): Seawater desalination plants using their products produce over 30 million m3/day worldwide (enough for 25%+ of U.S. population daily water needs). Products include High Pressure PX (20-400 gpm, 400-1200 psi), Ultra PX (10-250 gpm, 1200-1800 psi for wastewater/ZLD/MLD), Low Pressure PX (30-260 gpm, 80-400 psi for municipal reuse), hydraulic turbochargers (AT and LPT), and high-pressure pumps.
- Wastewater: Growing market with zero/minimum liquid discharge (ZLD/MLD) applications. Ultra PX addresses energy intensity and environmental impacts.
- Emerging Technologies: CO2-based refrigeration (PX G1300) leverages the pressure exchanger platform. HFC refrigerants are being phased down globally via the Kigali Amendment (85% reduction by 2036 in developed nations), and CO2 refrigeration is a climate-friendly alternative.

SALES CHANNELS:
1. Megaproject (MPD): Large-scale desalination plants >50,000 m3/day (13.2 million gallons/day), projects typically 16-36 months, revenue opportunities over $1 million each, majority of water treatment revenue.
2. Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM): Small-to-medium plants up to 50,000 m3/day, projects 1-16 months, revenue up to $1 million, capital expenditure driven.
3. Aftermarket (AM): Spare parts, repair services, field services, and commissioning for installed base.

COMPETITIVE POSITIONING:
The PX is said to have competitive advantages due to: (1) highly durable corrosion-resistant aluminum oxide (alumina) ceramic parts designed for 25+ year life, (2) warranty for high efficiencies in certain circumstances, (3) minimal unplanned/planned downtime with lower lifecycle cost, and (4) proven market track record.

SUSTAINABILITY:
The company's sustainability goals (announced in 2020 Sustainability Report) focus on four topics: Employees, Environmental & Climate Change Risks, Innovation & Opportunity, and Products. In 2023, the company announced its first corporate emissions reduction target, committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions as outlined in its 2022 Sustainability Report.

SIGNIFICANT FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS:
Key expectations include: continued industry-standard position in SWRO energy recovery; growth in wastewater markets due to expanding environmental regulations; technology conversion from thermal to RO in both desalination and wastewater; development of U.S. and China desalination markets; and commercial success of the PX G1300 in CO2 refrigeration. The report notes that a significant portion of revenue comes from outside the U.S., and there is no specific seasonality to desalination or wastewater revenue, though quarterly/yearly fluctuations occur primarily due to timing of MPD shipments. Forward-looking statements are based on information available as of February 21, 2024.

This technical paper documents the Madison Metropolitan Sewerage District's (MMSD) implementation of phosphorus recovery via struvite harvesting at its Nine Springs Wastewater Treatment Plant (NSWWTP) in Wisconsin, a 50 mgd (190,000 m³/d) advanced secondary treatment facility. The project, designed by Applied Technologies, Inc. (ATI) and implemented as part of the plant's "Eleventh Addition" beginning in 2010, aimed to address severe nuisance struvite (NH4MgPO4•6H2O) scaling problems that were causing maintenance issues in anaerobic digestion and dewatering equipment.

The system uses Ostara's Pearl® 2000 fluidized bed struvite harvesting reactors, with key components including: (1) two WAS blending/P-release tanks (1,140 m³ each) that convert intracellular phosphorus from enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) biomass into ortho-phosphate; (2) two mesophilic acid digesters (1,550 m³ each) that produce volatile fatty acids to promote phosphorus release; (3) separate filtrate management systems for WAS and digested sludge thickening operations; and (4) two Pearl® 2000 struvite reactors producing Crystal Green®, a slow-release fertilizer (5% N, 12% P as P2O5, 10% Mg). Operations began in October 2013.

RESULTS: The system achieved a 16% reduction in phosphorus load contained in Class B biosolids (from 852 to 718 kg/d, or 1,879 to 1,582 lb/d), with biosolids phosphorus content dropping from 3.8% to 3.4% (a 10% reduction). Revenues from harvested struvite increased to approximately $500/day in late 2016 (up from ~$325/day in 2014-2015), though below the design projection of ~$1,130/day. Maintenance cost savings from reduced nuisance struvite formation were estimated at approximately $1.3 million present worth.

DISCREPANCIES FROM DESIGN: Actual ortho-phosphate recovery in the reactors was below 50% for most of 2014-2016 versus the 77% design target, though recovery rates improved significantly from late 2015 through 2016 (reaching over 1,500 kg struvite/d and 190 kg P/d in the second half of 2016). Exogenous magnesium chloride consumption was nearly 250% of design (376 kg Mg/d vs. ~152 kg Mg/d expected), and ferric chloride savings were much lower than projected (only a 29% reduction vs. near-total elimination expected). Ferric chloride usage had to be maintained to control hydrogen sulfide in biogas and prevent nuisance struvite in digested sludge filtrate (since CO2 injection capacity was not used due to equipment complications). The WAS P-release system successfully converted over 80% of phosphorus in TWAS filtrate to ortho-phosphate, exceeding the design assumption of only 0.1% conversion. Actual flows to the harvester were 69% of design, and ortho-P loadings were 68% of design, while ammonia-N loadings were nearly double design projections.

The paper concludes that MMSD is poised to sustain its legacy of economic and ecological stewardship as phosphorus recovery rates continue to improve toward design targets, and recommends that future efforts carefully evaluate consequences of reduced ferric chloride consumption (e.g., hydrogen sulfide impacts on biogas).

<summary>
This webpage from Hazen and Sawyer describes a nutrient recovery project at the F. Wayne Hill Water Resources Center (FWHWRC) in Buford, GA. FWHWRC is a 60 mgd advanced wastewater treatment facility required to meet a stringent low phosphorus discharge limit of 0.08 mg/L. The facility switched to Mg(OH)2 in the collection system for odor and corrosion control, which led to struvite (NH4MgPO4•6H2O) formation becoming an operations and maintenance concern in the solids handling facilities.

To address struvite issues and the phosphorus limit, Gwinnett County undertook a pilot program and business case evaluation to assess two nutrient recovery technologies — Ostara Nutrient Recovery Technologies Inc. (using the Pearl® reactor with WASSTRIP) and Multiform Harvest Inc. Hazen and Sawyer assisted with comprehensive evaluation including bench and pilot scale testing, BioWin modeling, and net present cost analysis.

Nutrient recovery via struvite precipitation with continued Mg(OH)2 addition was found to be the most cost-effective alternative, with a payback period of just over 9 years over ferric treatment over a 20-year net present value analysis period. Sensitivity analyses showed that variations in ferric cost, inflation rate, discount rate, energy cost, and fertilizer revenue did not affect the overall ranking of alternatives.

WASSTRIP is described as a patented process that anaerobically reacts primary sludge (PS) with Bio-P waste activated sludge (WAS) to induce phosphorus release from phosphate accumulating microorganisms. Precipitating struvite as a slow-release fertilizer helps facilities meet lower phosphorus limits while creating a new revenue stream, mitigating operating costs and restoring a valuable resource as readily-minable phosphorus supply diminishes.

Project benefits include: meeting lower phosphorus limits while creating new revenue, validated pilot-scale technologies for phosphorus and ammonia recovery as fertilizer, and identification of the most appropriate treatment option via net present cost analysis. --- SOURCE 20: Phosphorus Recovery from Wastewater in the Circular Economy: Focus on Struvite Crystallization ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-8783/6/2/32

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Phosphorus Recovery from Wastewater in the Circular Economy: Focus on Struvite Crystallization

This is a critical narrative review published in the MDPI journal *Biomass* (2026, Volume 6, Issue 2, Article 32, DOI: 10.3390/biomass6020032) by Gergana Peeva from the Department of Chemical Technologies and Competence Center "Clean&Circle" at Burgas State University "Prof. Dr. Assen Zlatarov," Bulgaria. The article was submitted March 9, 2026, revised April 8, 2026, accepted April 10, 2026, and published April 17, 2026.

### Core Topic
The review provides a comprehensive synthesis of phosphorus recovery strategies from wastewater within a circular economy framework, with primary emphasis on struvite (MgNH4PO4·6H2O) crystallization as one of the most mature and practically implemented recovery routes. It positions struvite recovery against conventional, competing, and complementary pathways.

### Key Sections and Findings

**1. Phosphorus in Wastewater: Sources and Forms**
- Phosphorus enters wastewater from municipal (human excreta, detergents, food residues), agricultural (fertilizer use, livestock), and industrial (food processing, dairy, fertilizer manufacturing) sources.
- Typical total phosphorus concentrations in municipal wastewater range from 4 to 15 mg/L; sidestream flows (sludge dewatering liquors, anaerobic digestion effluents) can exceed 100 mg/L.
- Orthophosphate (o-PO4³⁻) is the most abundant, reactive, and recoverable phosphorus form. Phosphorus also exists as organic and particulate-bound forms.
- Phosphorus discharge causes eutrophication, algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and aquatic ecosystem degradation.

**2. Conventional Phosphorus Removal Technologies**
- **Enhanced Biological Phosphorus Removal (EBPR):** Uses polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (PAOs) under alternating anaerobic/aerobic conditions. Effective for compliance but transfers ~80–95% of influent phosphorus to sludge rather than recovering it. Performance sensitive to temperature, pH, sludge retention time, and carbon availability. EBPR can indirectly support struvite recovery by concentrating phosphorus in sludge that later releases it into sidestream liquors after digestion.
- **Chemical Precipitation:** Uses iron, aluminum, or calcium salts (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺, Ca²⁺) to form insoluble phosphates. Can exceed 95% removal efficiency but produces amorphous metal phosphates with low agronomic value and limited reuse potential.

**3. Recovery from Sewage Sludge Ash (SSA)**
- Incineration reduces sludge mass/volume by 70–90%, concentrating phosphorus in ash at ~10–25% P2O5.
- **Wet-chemical leaching** (H2SO4, HCl, H3PO4): Can achieve >90% extraction but co-dissolves heavy metals (Cd, Pb, Cu) requiring purification. Example: EcoPhos.
- **Thermochemical routes** (800–1000°C with MgCl2/CaCl2): Volatilize heavy metals and transform phosphorus into bioavailable phases (renanite-type). Examples: AshDec, Mephrec. Higher energy demand but cleaner products.

**4. Struvite Crystallization (MgNH4PO4·6H2O)**
- Formation driven by supersaturation; ionic activity product (IAP) must exceed solubility product constant (Ksp), with reported Ksp values ranging from 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁴.
- Two stages: nucleation and crystal growth, with the relative dominance determining crystal size distribution and morphology.
- Produces a slow-release fertilizer containing phosphorus, nitrogen, and magnesium; mitigates uncontrolled scaling in pipelines and dewatering equipment.
- Most robust performance occurs in high-strength sidestreams (digester supernatant, dewatering centrate/filtrate), where supersaturation potential and process controllability are favorable.
- Key challenges include: magnesium supply and cost, competition with calcium phosphate formation, sensitivity to organic matter and ionic strength, wastewater matrix effects, and mainstream application feasibility.

**5. Regulatory Context**
- EU Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 provides a pathway for placing recovered fertilizers on the market under defined quality and safety criteria, including precipitated phosphate salts and related recovered materials.

**6. Conclusions**
- Controlled sidestream struvite crystallization offers the most favorable balance between recovery efficiency, operational reliability, and fertilizer product quality under suitable plant conditions.
- Recovery technology selection must be guided by stream characteristics (mainstream vs. sidestream), sludge management infrastructure, product requirements, and local regulatory/market context.
- SSA recovery is a complementary rather than universal replacement option, most relevant where mono-incineration is established.
- The novelty of this review lies in integrating process fundamentals, reactor technologies, implementation evidence, product quality, environmental/economic performance, and regulatory context within a single WRRF-oriented framework.

### Keywords
struvite; phosphorus recovery; wastewater treatment; circular economy; nutrient recovery; bio-based fertilizers; resource recovery
</summary>

"Controlled sidestream struvite crystallization appears to offer the most favorable balance between recovery efficiency, operational reliability, and fertilizer product quality under suitable plant conditions."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.takadu.com/blog/from-the-field-delving-into-dmas-and-devices

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is part of TaKaDu's "From the Field" series, featuring interviews with water utility operators about their District Metered Area (DMA) strategies, monitoring devices, and future plans. The piece includes insights from six water utility professionals across Chile, Australia, and Peru.

**DMA Strategies and Current Operations:**

- **Rhett Duncan (Unitywater, Queensland, Australia):** Operates ~180 DMAs with 2,000-4,000 properties each. Rolling out a "digital neighborhood" with 10,000 smart meters across three DMAs, integrating flow meters, pressure monitoring, acoustic leak detection, and water quality sensors. About 8,000 smart meters already installed. Acoustic leak detection identified leaks totaling ~160 million liters that would have gone unnoticed. The trial is focused on building a business case for the other 176 DMAs and testing how to handle the volume of data.

- **Francisco Iturriaga (Esval & Aquas del Valle, Chile):** Operates over 7,000 km of potable water, 50+ wastewater treatment plants, 80+ potable water plants, and 900,000+ customers. Hilly topography requires 1,000+ pressure reducing valves. Sectorization began in 2014, now ~460 DMAs with 8,000+ sensors generating ~100 events monthly in TaKaDu.

- **Nick Goninan (Hunter Water, NSW, Australia):** Began DMA rollout in 2015-16 with a goal to reduce real losses by 2.4 gigalitres per year by 2024 and increase DMA coverage from 25% to 100%. Reached 45% coverage in 2021 with 120 flow meters; anticipates needing 200 more. Aims for DMAs under 5,000 properties.

- **Germán Ramos (Sedapal, Peru):** Sectorization in Lima began in 1994, dividing the city into sectors averaging 5,000 connections over ~25 km². Now has ~400 sectors with SCADA remote control. Non-revenue water reduced from ~48% in the 1990s to ~23% today. Installing GPS-enabled data loggers for pressure management.

- **Darren Cash (Sydney Water, Australia):** Serves 5+ million customers; ~25% of network divided into pressure-managed DMAs set up between 2007-2010. Found ~5,000 properties per DMA is the "sweet spot." Pressure management resulted in 4-5% reduction in breaks and leakage per zone. DMAs allow real-time leak detection and targeted investigations rather than blind active-leak detection.

- **Cristian Jiménez (Aguas Antofagasta, Chile):** Network is "born sectorized" due to challenging terrain (200m altitude differences over just 3-4 km). Before TaKaDu (2011), had one sensor per 6-7 km; has since tripled sensor numbers.

**Future Plans:**

- Unitywater plans to continue smart meter rollout, eventually converting all meters (turned over every ~15 years) within 10-15 years. Also testing sewer network smart monitoring to address tidal inundation, infiltration, and inflow challenges (treated ~10% more water than sold last year).
- Hunter Water plans to further segment networks, use virtual DMAs, and use TaKaDu to direct active leak detection rather than sweeping. Trialing residential smart meters for billing integration.
- Sedapal plans to implement a big data analysis system to complement existing sectorization.
- Sydney Water aims for at least one pressure sensor per isolation block of 20-30 properties through digital meter rollout.

The article concludes with a TaKaDu team note emphasizing that DMAs are fundamental to effective water network management, and links to a related article on calculating ideal DMA size.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This initiative is not about proving the technology, as we know it works. Rather, it's now about testing it en masse, and critically to help us build a business case to go forward to roll it out across the other 176 DMAs in the organization." - Rhett Duncan, Unitywater

"Pressure management has resulted in a 4% to 5% reduction in the number of breaks and leakage within each zone. But one of the key things that the DMAs allow us to do is really to get a better handle on the leakage as it's happening, and to target investigations rather than just doing blind active-leak detection, which is the traditional approach." - Darren Cash, Sydney Water

"We have a hilly topography and our water production catchment is far from the distribution areas, so we need many pressure reducing valves – over 1000 – to maintain the pressure within the allowed ranges." - Francisco Iturriaga, Esval & Aquas del Valle

"This has allowed us to reduce non-revenue water, which in the 1990s was around 48%, to the current level of around 23%." - Germán Ramos, Sedapal

"I'm convinced that sectorization alone is important, but it is more important if there were a tool that manages the big data that it creates." - Germán Ramos, Sedapal

--- SOURCE 4: 5 Hidden Challenges for Water Utilities – Insights from the Field – TaKaDu ---
URL: https://www.takadu.com/blog/5-hidden-challenges-for-water-utilities-insights-from-the-field

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Amir Peleg, Founder & CEO of TaKaDu (published October 28, 2020), outlines seven layers of hidden challenges facing water utilities, drawn from over a decade of experience implementing Central Event Management (CEM) systems globally. TaKaDu provides a SaaS-based CEM solution using smart analytics to help water distribution utilities reduce water loss, improve operational efficiency, and increase customer satisfaction.

The seven layers of challenges are structured from most visible to most obscured:

**Visible layers (NRW challenges):**
1. **Physical water losses** – Leakage from transmission/distribution mains, storage tanks, and service connections. Early detection and quantification can save millions, especially including energy wastage.
2. **Apparent water losses** – Unauthorized consumption and inaccurate meters. A large Australian utility discovered a pipe leaking for over two years via its first CEM alert; the system prevented approximately 6.5 billion liters of water loss (annualized calculation).

**Less-visible layers:**
3. **Data quality** – Many utilities assume sensors work correctly; one customer discovered 30% of relatively new sensors were not functioning. Utilities also struggle with "data tsunami" – overwhelming volumes of data they cannot scale to handle.
4. **Operational efficiency** – Resource allocation is often poor. A South American utility with high false-alarm rates had every 100 leak detection jobs yield 40 dry holes; after CEM implementation (single view, DMA-based leak boundaries, cross-department communication), the dry hole rate dropped by 50%.
5. **Customer satisfaction and quality of service** – CEM systems provide pinpoint visibility into hidden leaks, water quality events, and pressure events, enabling faster response and shorter repair cycles. A regional utility in Spain halved repair time for invisible leaks.
6. **Data and knowledge retention** – Utilities face challenges replacing aging workforce expertise. CEM systems help cover skill and knowledge shortfalls via automatic event detection, unified dashboards, and historical event logs.
7. **Planning challenges** – Limited proactive maintenance planning. CEM enables strategic decisions on investment prioritization and maintenance scheduling, reducing reactive actions.

The article emphasizes that most utilities initially pursue CEM for NRW reduction but discover the deeper, less-obvious challenges through implementation. It includes a link to a webinar recording and is also available in Spanish.
</summary>

New service-based business models like network-as-a-service (NaaS) and metering-as-a-service (MaaS) are broadening market access for smaller or budget-constrained utilities by reducing up-front capital investments. Retrofit technologies such as meter interface units are extending digital capabilities to legacy meters, connecting to IoT networks like Amazon Sidewalk to expand smart metering to rural and hard-to-reach areas.

Policy remains a double-edged sword. In Europe, supportive programs like Spain's €3 billion PERTE initiative and the U.K.'s AMP8 mandate to install 10 million smart meters by 2030 are driving large-scale rollouts. The U.S. has a more mixed environment: federal infrastructure funding provides momentum, but tariffs and Build America, Buy America (BABA) rules pressure manufacturing and supply chains. A temporary BABA waiver for AMI meters remains in place through 2027, though longer-term compliance requires considerable investment in domestic electronic component sourcing.

The findings come from Bluefield Research's Insight Report, "Global Water Metering Outlook: Evolving Technology Trends, Business Models, Competitive Landscape, and Leading Companies," drawing on over a decade of proprietary research, industry interviews, utility case studies, and financial analysis. The report is available for purchase or with a Digital Water Landscape Corporate Subscription.
</summary>

- A 2017-2020 survey of 194 representative water enterprises showed widespread attention and high value recognition for digital water construction.

--- SOURCE 1: Interview: digital trends in the Chinese water market | Aquatech ---
URL: https://www.aquatechtrade.com/water-stories/water-treatment/china-ai-digital-water-market-challenges-opportunties

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is an interview with Bruno Lhopiteau, managing director of Siveco China and Bluebee Tech, about digital trends in the Chinese water market. Published by Aquatech Online on Tuesday, 23 September 2025.

Key findings from the interview:

- China is among the world's fastest adopters of digital tools in the water sector, driven by government mandates like the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025). By 2024, more than 90% of urban water utilities adopted 'basic' IoT sensors for real-time monitoring. The 'Digital Water' initiative post-2020 led to Smart Water solutions in 70% of new wastewater treatment plants for predictive maintenance and leak detection. Investments exceed €10 billion annually, outpacing global averages (around 40% in Europe per IWA reports).

- Despite impressive statistics, Lhopiteau notes that many 'smart' projects did not deliver real operational outputs, with "smart money" going to non-core systems (intelligent parking, facial recognition, cosmetic SCADA upgrades) or failed IT developments.

- Intense competition characterized the market: every big water company invested heavily in IT aiming to spin off divisions and list on the stock market, while countless IoT, SCADA, GIS, and IT providers fought price wars—many did not survive. The COVID period and lack of infrastructure stimulus caused significant financing issues and restructuring, though the market is showing signs of recovery.

- Chinese firms stand out for their ability to accumulate experience quickly despite high failure rates. Investment will continue, propelling water technologies globally as Chinese firms get more involved in international projects.

- Smart water technologies (Digital Twins, 3D BIM models, IoT, BI tools) are widely adopted. Competition keeps costs relatively low. Surviving vendors will emerge as local and global players.

- Lhopiteau's French company reinvented both its technology and business model through two decades in the Chinese water market, becoming more resilient and battle-tested for global competition.

- AI use is progressing: algorithms for real-time contaminant detection claim 95% accuracy in pathogen identification; AI-powered acoustic sensors claim 85% leak detection in Beijing's network (non-revenue water losses up to 30% nationally); Beijing piloted swarm robot technology for sludge removal and pipe cleaning with efficiency gains up to 40%.

- China is the world leader in scalable IoT and big data, with projects over one million IoT devices in urban water networks (e.g., Shenzhen). AI for flood and drought management is claimed to reach accuracy levels far superior to the West.

- Three opportunity areas for international companies: 1) the Foreign Investment Encouraged Catalogue (NDRC/MOFCOM policy encouraging foreign expertise and investment in water); 2) the Belt and Road Initiative opening avenues for business with Chinese firms in overseas projects (Southeast Asia, Africa); 3) rural water infrastructure with multilateral agency funding (e.g., World Bank), though Lowest-Priced Technically Acceptable tenders favor local players.

- China lags in interoperability and standardisation (data silos, slow ISO 50001 adoption), though Lhopiteau views this as temporary, citing China's early involvement in designing ISO 55000 (national standard GB/T 33172) and its capacity for fast standardisation demonstrated in power generation.

- The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), currently in drafting, emphasizes AI for 'new quality productive forces' in water with indications of €50+ billion investment for 'water security' amid climate risks. Likely outcomes include AI mandates, potential calls for increased international firm involvement in PPP projects (currently only Suez, Veolia, and Sembcorp remain as foreign water players in China), continued priorities on rural infrastructure and cutting water losses, and water tech exports via Belt and Road.

The article also promotes Aquatech China, the leading water technology trade show in China, running November 5-7 in Shanghai.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Adoption accelerated post-2020 with the 'Digital Water' initiative, with Smart Water solutions deployed in 70 per cent of new wastewater treatment plants for predictive maintenance and leak detection." - Lhopiteau
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: How innovative solutions help Veolia to drive ecological transformation with its stakeholders ---
URL: https://journals.openedition.org/factsreports/7249

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Field Actions Science Reports (Special Issue 25, 2023, pp. 48-53), is written by Catherine Ricou, Head of Innovation at Veolia. It explores how Veolia uses innovative solutions to drive ecological transformation with its stakeholders. Ricou became Head of Innovation in 2022, is a graduate of AgroParisTech with over 25 years of experience in environmental management (water, waste, and energy recovery), and now leads innovation for the combined Veolia-Suez scope.

KEY FACTS AND CONTEXT:
- Veolia has set a target to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, invested 165 million euros in 2022, operates 14 R&D centers globally, and holds nearly 5,000 patents.
- In 2022, Veolia published its new statement of purpose: "We develop and implement locally solutions to depollute our vital resources and preserve them from depletion, solutions to decarbonize our ways of living and producing and adapt them to the consequences of climate change."
- In 2022, Veolia's actions helped avoid 14 MtCO2 emissions and saved 320 million m³ of water compared to 2019 through reducing network leakages.
- Veolia weights and rates all new innovation solutions regarding their net contribution to ecological transformation.

MAJOR INNOVATION PILLARS AND EXAMPLES:
1. CIRCULAR MATERIALS: Veolia is circularizing electric vehicle battery production (from mechanical recycling to refining lithium and strategic metals) and developed Plastiloop, the first global integrated platform for circular polymers with 37 plastic recycling plants worldwide. Plastiloop's key innovation is its demand-based approach—starting with the end product and customer requirements rather than "recycling waste and finding uses for it."

2. DEPOLLUTION: Roughly 33% of the world's soil is degraded (per FAO), largely due to chemical fertilizer overuse. Veolia has developed technologies including zero-liquid discharge solutions, reverse osmosis processes, and flue gas treatment, while also working to minimize secondary environmental impacts (energy footprint and supplemental chemicals) of these treatments.

3. GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE: Veolia is shifting from gray to green-and-gray infrastructure. The Urban Flood Park La Marjal in Alicante, Spain (3.6 hectares), a 50-50 joint venture between Aguas de Alicante and Alicante City Council, protects against flooding while reviving biodiversity. It features Mediterranean native vegetation, two purpose-built ponds mimicking Mediterranean wetlands, water retention, a circular water management system with cascade oxygenation and aerators, with shared operation between the City Council and Aguas de Alicante.

4. FROM VOLUME TO VALUE: On May 11, 2023, Veolia renewed a contract to supply water to the Lille metropolitan area for ten years—the first in France to stipulate a 10% reduction in water consumption with financial penalties if unmet. Veolia will install 5,000 sensors/probes, renew nearly 12,000 drinking water connections, use the "leak alert" system via Vig'iléo (an extension of Hubgrade hypervision centers) to detect leaks within 48 hours, provide "consumption coaches" to 1.2 million consumers, and aim to finalize 1,200 water-saving contracts targeting 15% reduction each.

CULTIVATING INNOVATION SPIRIT:
- INSIDE: Veolia (220,000+ employees) launched the Innovation Academy in 2022 to boost innovative mindsets, develop innovation programs across business units, and train all employees.
- OUTSIDE: Veolia develops Open Innovation ecosystems, invests in start-up incubators (e.g., PureControl for optimizing energy consumption in wastewater treatment plants), and partners with scientific and academic institutions.

CONCLUSION: Ricou argues that innovation combines technological and business model innovations, and that any company can adopt the principle of supporting others' ecological transformation through deep investment in people, fostering an innovation mindset, and working outside organizational walls for speed and scale—adopting business models where "your company does well when the planet benefits."
</summary>

The project addresses the challenge of underground water leaks—in 2022, Singapore experienced an average of 4.1 reported water leaks per 100km of pipe, most of which were underground and hidden. PUB deployed hundreds of monitoring stations across the city's underground water pipes as part of its Smart Water Grid (SWG) initiative, creating a live digital twin of the water network using real-time sensor updates maintained around the clock. Engineers then applied machine learning to the sensor data to refine predictive analysis models and continuously update them, enabling the modeling and prediction of flows and pressures, tracking the health status of different zones, and continuously recalibrating and retraining the digital twin. This capability, called the Anomaly Leak Finder (ALF), detects anomalies—especially hidden leaks and pipe bursts—and locates them for field crews. ALF was benchmarked with historical data to validate its effectiveness, and in 2024 it detected two operational leaks that were verified by field crews. The major economic gain for PUB is reduced time spent on manual inspections (which are time-consuming and ineffective for hidden underground leaks), replaced by monitoring the water network through the live digital twin constantly updated by sensor data.
</summary>

**Acwa** (formerly ACWA Power)[[1]](#cite_note-1) is a developer, investor, co-owner and operator of a portfolio of power generation and desalinated water production plants with a presence in 14 countries across the Middle East, Africa, and Central and Southeast Asia. Acwa's portfolio of projects in operation and development has an investment value of USD 107.5 billion, and a capacity of 78.85 GW of power and produces 9.5 million m3 /day of desalinated water.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)

Its energy portfolio includes thermal power plants,[[3]](#cite_note-3) solar power plants (photovoltaic (PV) and [concentrated solar power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentrated_solar_power "Concentrated solar power") (CSP)),[[4]](#cite_note-4) [wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_power "Wind power"),[[5]](#cite_note-5) water [desalination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desalination "Desalination") plants,[[6]](#cite_note-6) and [green hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_hydrogen "Green hydrogen") projects.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-CompanyOverviewQuote-8)

## Background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ACWA_Power&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Headquartered in Saudi Arabia, ACWA Power maintains regional offices in Riyadh, Jeddah, Dubai, Baku, Beijing, Cairo, Addis Abbaba, Jakarta, Amman, Rabat, Muscat, Johannesburg, Istanbul, Tashkent, and Hanoi.[[9]](#cite_note-9) It invests in, develops, co-owns and operates a portfolio of +100 projects with the capacity of 78.85 GW of power and produce 9.5 million m3 /day of desalinated water.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) ACWA Power and its subsidiary operating companies employ around 4,000 people in projects in 14 different countries.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In January 2026, the company officially changed its trading name from ACWA Power to Acwa and unveiled a new brand identity. This rebranding marked the company’s transition from a regional Saudi Arabian developer to a global infrastructure platform managing over US$115 billion in assets across 15 countries. The refreshed identity is built around the "energy quadrilemma" of affordability, sustainability, security, and speed. Coinciding with the rebrand, Acwa announced a strategic goal to double its [assets under management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assets_under_management "Assets under management") to US$250 billion by 2030, focusing on large-scale green hydrogen, next-generation desalination, and renewable energy storage.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

## Structure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ACWA_Power&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Structure")]

ACWA Power's board of directors is chaired by Mohammad Abdullah Abunayyan,[[13]](#cite_note-13) with Raad Al Saady as its Vice Chairman and Managing Director,[[14]](#cite_note-14) and Marco Arcelli as its CEO.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=ACWA_Power&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

In 2002, the Government of Saudi Arabia changed the regulations so that the private sector was permitted to own and operate utilities such as water and power plants. The company was originally founded in 2004 as ACWA Power Projects, a joint venture between ACWA Holding (representing the [Abunayyan Holding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abunayyan_Holding?action=edit&redlink=1 "Abunayyan Holding (page does not exist)") Company and [Al-Muhaidib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Muhaidib "Al-Muhaidib"), today known as Vision International Investment Company) and the MADA Group for Industrial and Commercial Development (today known as Al Rajhi Group Holding) to take advantage of these new private sector investment and operation opportunities in the Saudi Arabian market. The company was reorganised in 2008 in its current legal form as ACWA Power Company.[[16]](#cite_note-ACWAPowerBornSaudiGrowingGlobally-16) From 2004 to 2011, ACWA Power focused primarily on Saudi Arabia, and was awarded contracts for several thermal power projects – including the Shuaibah IWPP, Shuqaiq 2 IWPP, Rabigh IPP and Marafiq IPP.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) The company began international expansion in 2011 with the acquisition of Central Electricity Generating Company (CEGCO) in Jordan, and the signature of a joint development agreement for the Kirikkale Combined Cycle Gas Turbine project in Turkey, which subsequently won backing from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) Today, ACWA Power operates across 14 countries in the Middle East, Africa, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia, with a portfolio comprising renewable energy, water desalination, green hydrogen, and conventional energy projects.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

In 2018, the [Public Investment Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Investment_Fund "Public Investment Fund") (PIF) of Saudi Arabia acquired a 15% stake in ACWA Power and has progressively increased its shareholding to 44%, reinforcing ACWA Power’s pivotal role in achieving the Kingdom’s Vision 2030 [energy transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_transition "Energy transition") goals.[[26]](#cite_note-26)
