From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Brand of reclaimed wastewater

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/NEWater.jpg/250px-NEWater.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NEWater.jpg)

Bottles of NEWater for distribution during the [National Day Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_National_Day_Parade "Singapore National Day Parade") celebrations of 2005 at [Marina South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marina_South "Marina South")

 [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/NEWater_Bottle_NDP_2014.jpeg/250px-NEWater_Bottle_NDP_2014.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NEWater_Bottle_NDP_2014.jpeg)

Bottle of NEWater that was given out during NDP 2014.

**NEWater** (pronounced New-Water) is the brand name given to [highly treated reclaimed wastewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reclaimed_water "Reclaimed water") produced by [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore")'s [Public Utilities Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Utilities_Board "Public Utilities Board"). NEWater is produced by further purifying conventionally treated [wastewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wastewater "Wastewater") through [microfiltration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfiltration "Microfiltration"), [reverse osmosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_osmosis "Reverse osmosis") and ultraviolet radiation. The water is potable quality and can be added to drinking water supply reservoirs where it is withdrawn and treated again in conventional water treatment plants before being distributed to consumers. However, most NEWater is currently used for non-drinking purposes, mostly by industries with production requirements for high purity water.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=NEWater&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Singapore considered water recycling to augment its limited fresh water supply starting in the 1970s.[[1]](#cite_note-1) A Master Plan drafted in 1972 identified water reclamation and desalination as alternatives to reduce dependence on imported water from Malaysia. Subsequently, an experimental water reclamation treatment plant was built in 1974, but the operation was terminated after only one year due to costs and reliability issues.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

In 1998, the Public Utilities Board (PUB) and the [Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Environment_and_Water_Resources "Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources") (MEWR) initiated the Singapore Water Reclamation Study (NEWater Study).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The aim was to determine if NEWater was a viable source of raw water for Singapore's needs. NEWater and [desalination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desalination "Desalination") both were explored to reduce reliance on water imported from [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), which has long been a source of friction between the Malaysian and Singapore governments.[[4]](#cite_note-4) The Malaysian government is treaty-bound to sell water to Singapore until 2061, but it has no obligation to do so after that date.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In 2001, PUB initiated efforts to identify non-potable uses of water. NEWater, because of its high quality, became the supply of choice for industry demands. This use provided an outlet for this new water supply without increasing the demand on the limited potable water supply.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The PUB launched NEWater to the public in 2003, with the opening of the first two NEWater plants - the Bedok and Kranji plants - as well as the NEWater Visitor Centre.[[7]](#cite_note-7) In anticipation of the potential public concerns over the safety of recycled water, NEWater was carefully implemented. The PUB was cautious in its usage of terms, avoiding terms such as 'wastewater' or 'sewage' that carried a negative connotation.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Sewage treatment plants were renamed to 'water reclamation plants' and sewage or wastewater were referred to as 'used water'. This contributed to a positive framing of NEWater, enhancing public acceptance of reused water. In addition, the government extensively engaged the public through exhibitions and advertisements to educate them about NEWater. The NEWater Visitor Centre, which allows people to view the NEWater treatment process, was also opened to enhance visitors' understanding of how NEWater is produced. These public engagement efforts were aimed at correcting any misunderstandings people might have towards recycled water and increasing public support for reused water.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Also, innovative technologies which was promoted by international industries applied on NEWater, such as [LG Chem](https://www.lgwatersolutions.com/en/main)[[10]](#cite_note-10) and [DuPont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont "DuPont")[[11]](#cite_note-11) in its reverse osmosis technologies.

## Production

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=NEWater&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Production")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/NEWater_S.C.A.D.A._room.jpg/250px-NEWater_S.C.A.D.A._room.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NEWater_S.C.A.D.A._room.jpg)

Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (S.C.A.D.A.) room at a NEWater plant

 [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/NEWater_Bedok_plant.jpg/250px-NEWater_Bedok_plant.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NEWater_Bedok_plant.jpg)

Bedok NEWater Factory

The first NEWater plant was completed in May 2000. Singapore currently has four operational NEWater factories, at Bedok, Kranji, Ulu Pandan and Changi. The Bedok and Kranji factories were commissioned in 2002, the Ulu Pandan plant in March 2007 and the Changi plant in August 2009.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) A plant at Seletar, commissioned in February 2004, was closed in 2011,[[14]](#cite_note-14) as the PUB implemented its plan to centralize the treatment of used water, under the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System.[[15]](#cite_note-15) In January 2017, a new NEWater plant was launched at [Changi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changi "Changi"), and is the first plant to be jointly developed by a foreign and local company.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

The Bedok and Kranji plants are operated by the Public Utilities Board, while the Ulu Pandan and Changi plants are under [DBOO concessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build–operate–transfer "Build–operate–transfer") by Keppel Seghers[[17]](#cite_note-17) and [Sembcorp Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sembcorp_Industries "Sembcorp Industries").[[18]](#cite_note-18)

There is a Visitor Centre in the NEWater factory in Bedok, near the Singapore Expo [Tanah Merah MRT station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanah_Merah_MRT_station "Tanah Merah MRT station"). The visitor centre was awarded the Best Sightseeing/Leisure/Educational Programme at the 20th Tourism Awards 2005 and the IWA Marketing & Communication Award in 2006.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

The visitor centre provides multiple free programmes to educate the public regarding the technologies and production of NEWater:

* NEWater Scientist Program – Students take on the role of NEWater Scientists and explore the visitor centre[[20]](#cite_note-20)
* Outdoor Classroom – Host fun activities and experiments that help students learn about reverse osmosis and other NEWater processes[[21]](#cite_note-21)
* Water Ambassadors – Small workshops that teach uniformed groups (i.e. National Cadet Corps and Scouts Association) skills to be water ambassadors[[22]](#cite_note-22)

### Procedure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=NEWater&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Procedure")]

NEWater source water comes from [effluent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effluent "Effluent") of [secondary sewage treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_treatment "Secondary treatment") plants.[[31]](#cite_note-31) The effluent passes through a multiple-barrier water reclamation process:[[32]](#cite_note-32)[[33]](#cite_note-mbr-33)

* The first stage of the NEWater production process uses [microfiltration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfiltration "Microfiltration")/[ultrafiltration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultrafiltration "Ultrafiltration") to remove suspended solids, colloidal particles, disease-causing bacteria, some [viruses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viruses "Viruses") and [protozoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protozoan "Protozoan") [cysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbial_cyst "Microbial cyst"). The filtered water after passing through the membrane contains only dissolved salts and organic molecules.
* The second stage of the NEWater production process uses [reverse osmosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_osmosis "Reverse osmosis") (RO). A [semi-permeable membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-permeable_membrane "Semi-permeable membrane") filters out contaminants such as bacteria, viruses, [heavy metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metals "Heavy metals"), [nitrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate "Nitrate"), [chlorides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloride "Chloride"), [sulfates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulphate "Sulphate"), disinfection by-products, aromatic hydrocarbons, and [pesticides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pesticides "Pesticides"). NEWater is thus free from viruses and bacteria and contains very low levels of salts and [organic matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_matter "Organic matter"). At this stage, the water is of potable quality.
* The third stage of the NEWater production process is a safety precaution. [UV disinfection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet#Sterilization_and_disinfection "Ultraviolet") is used to ensure that all organisms are inactivated and the purity of the water can be guaranteed. After adding some alkaline chemicals to restore the [pH balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH_balance "PH balance"), NEWater is ready for use.

* NEWater production process
* [![Microfiltration system](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Microfiltration_system_at_Bedok_NEWater_Factory.jpg/250px-Microfiltration_system_at_Bedok_NEWater_Factory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Microfiltration_system_at_Bedok_NEWater_Factory.jpg "Microfiltration system")

## Applications

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=NEWater&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Applications")]

The total capacity of the plants is about 200 million US gallons per day (760,000 m3/d). About 6% of this is used for [indirect potable use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indirect_potable_use "Indirect potable use"), equal to about 1% of Singapore's potable water requirement of 380 million US gallons per day (1,400,000 m3/d). The rest is used at [wafer fabrication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wafer_fabrication "Wafer fabrication") plants and other non-[potable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potable "Potable") applications in industries in [Woodlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlands,_Singapore "Woodlands, Singapore"), [Tampines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampines "Tampines"), [Pasir Ris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasir_Ris "Pasir Ris"), and [Ang Mo Kio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ang_Mo_Kio "Ang Mo Kio").

Government figures show that the country's NEWater plans can meet up to 40% of Singapore's current needs, and the figure is expected to go up to 55% by 2060.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

### Potability

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=NEWater&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Potability")]

The quality of NEWater consistently exceeds the requirements set by [USEPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency") and [WHO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") guidelines and is cleaner than other water sources in Singapore.[[35]](#cite_note-faq-35)

args.summary:
NEWater is the brand name for highly treated reclaimed wastewater produced by Singapore's Public Utilities Board (PUB). It is created by further purifying conventionally treated wastewater through a three-stage process: microfiltration/ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis, and ultraviolet radiation with pH-balancing alkaline chemicals. The water is of potable quality and can be added to drinking water reservoirs, though most is used for non-drinking purposes by industries requiring high-purity water.

**History:** Singapore explored water recycling since the 1970s to reduce dependence on imported water from Malaysia. An experimental plant in 1974 was terminated after one year due to costs and reliability. In 1998, the PUB and Ministry of the Environment initiated the Singapore Water Reclamation Study (NEWater Study). The first plants (Bedok and Kranji) opened in 2003 along with the NEWater Visitor Centre. To build public acceptance, PUB deliberately avoided negative terms like 'wastewater' or 'sewage', renaming treatment plants as 'water reclamation plants' and referring to sewage as 'used water'. Innovative reverse osmosis technologies from companies like LG Chem and DuPont were applied.

**Production:** Four NEWater factories currently operate in Singapore: Bedok (decommissioned 31 July 2024), Kranji (commissioned 2002), Ulu Pandan (2007, operated by Keppel Seghers), and Changi (2017, operated by BEWG-UESH; also Sembcorp plant at Changi commissioned 2010). A Seletar plant operated from 2004 until decommissioned in 2011. The Bedok plant's Visitor Centre offers free educational programs (NEWater Scientist Program, Outdoor Classroom, Water Ambassadors) and won the Best Sightseeing/Leisure/Educational Programme at the 2005 Tourism Awards.

The production procedure: (1) microfiltration/ultrafiltration removes suspended solids, bacteria, viruses, and protozoan cysts; (2) reverse osmosis filters out bacteria, viruses, heavy metals, nitrates, chlorides, sulfates, disinfection by-products, and pesticides; (3) UV disinfection inactivates organisms and alkaline chemicals restore pH balance.

**Applications:** Total plant capacity is about 200 million US gallons per day (760,000 m³/d). About 6% is used for indirect potable use (~1% of Singapore's potable water requirement of 380 million US gallons/day). The rest serves wafer fabrication plants and other industries in Woodlands, Tampines, Pasir Ris, and Ang Mo Kio. NEWater can meet up to 40% of Singapore's current needs, projected to reach 55% by 2060.

**Potability:** NEWater quality consistently exceeds USEPA and WHO guidelines and is cleaner than other water sources in Singapore, with parameters like turbidity <5 NTU, pH 7.0–8.5, and undetectable total coliform bacteria.

args.summary: This webpage is an informational video by Singapore's Public Utilities Board (PUB) about NEWater, Singapore's high-grade reclaimed water program, posted on August 2, 2016. NEWater is produced from treated used water that undergoes a rigorous three-stage purification process: (1) microfiltration to remove suspended solids, minute particles, bacteria, and viruses; (2) reverse osmosis, where a semi-permeable membrane with very small pores filters the water so only water molecules pass through; and (3) ultraviolet disinfection as an additional safety barrier. NEWater is ultra-clean, safe to drink, and primarily used for industrial and air cooling purposes, with a small amount used to top up raw water reservoirs when needed. Its biggest users are wafer fabrication plants, which require stringent water quality standards. NEWater has passed more than 130,000 scientific tests and is well within the World Health Organization's guidelines. PUB recognized that public acceptance was key to success and launched public engagement campaigns involving grassroots leaders, water experts, businesses, schools, and the general public. The NEWater Visitor Centre, a state-of-the-art water museum with interactive tours and educational workshops, was established to maintain public understanding and support. A 2002 independent poll showed 98% of respondents would drink NEWater, demonstrating overwhelming public acceptance. NEWater strengthens Singapore's water supply resilience against dry weather and has become a pillar of Singapore's water sustainability strategy thanks to strong political will and continual investment in water research and development.

In 2025, the global economy was characterised by many national economies showing slow or no growth. Coinciding with this, geopolitical tensions led to greater uncertainty and, consequently, lower investment appetite. We did, on the other hand, experience continued challenges in China, where a depressed construction sector and fierce competition impact our business. Financial risks 

As a result of our global activities, group profit and equity are influenced by a number of financial risks. Foreign exchange risks in the operating companies are managed centrally, as are interest and liquidity risks. The Board of Directors has set up a policy for the use of financial instruments. 

Foreign exchange risk 

Grundfos’ policy is to hedge foreign exchange rates for the most essential flow of goods, i.e. sale and purchase of goods. The objective of the policy is to reduce the potential adverse short-term (up to 18 months) impact of foreign exchange rate fluctuations on cash flows and earnings, and thereby allow for planning and counteractions in the case of longer-term adverse impacts. Currency hedging is carried out centrally by Group Treasury and covers cash flow risk as well as fair value risk. Cash flow risk is hedged for a peri-od of up to 18 months, aiming at a coverage of 50 – 90% of the expected exposure, whereas fair value hedging aims at 80 – 90% coverage of the balance sheet exposure. The most important currencies hedged are USD, AUD, GBP, CNY and HUF. At the end of 2025, currency contracts to reduce the foreign exchange risk in connection with the flow of goods amounted to DKK 6,630m (2024: DKK 6,760m). Reference is made to Note 31 for further details. 

Other financial risks • Liquidity risk: Financial independence is a core value for Grundfos. Maintaining adequate liquidity is therefore key. In addition to unused borrowing facilities, net deposits amounted to DKK 6,774m by the end of 2025 (2024: DKK 8,174m). 

• Credit risk: Credit risks derive primarily from trade debtors, securities and bank receivables. Risks on trade debtors are diversified across a large number of customers, reducing the exposure. • Raw materials risk: Grundfos does not hedge raw materials. No single raw material constitutes a significant proportion of production costs.

## Grundfos Annual Report 2025 — Key Summary

**Overview & Reporting Framework**
The Grundfos Annual Report 2025 is the first to combine financial and sustainability performance in a single report. Prepared in accordance with IFRS as adopted by the EU and the Danish Financial Statements Act, it includes management's review, sustainability statements, and consolidated financial statements. While Grundfos is not yet in scope of the EU CSRD, the sustainability statements serve as a preparatory step toward full CSRD compliance from financial year 2027, reflecting ESRS principles and double materiality assessments. The report is structured around: Management's Review, Sustainability Statements, and Consolidated Financial Statements, covering governance, purpose/strategy, performance, and material topics including water stewardship, water access, climate transition, circularity, people, and governance/integrity.

**CEO Letter (Poul Due Jensen)**
- 2025 marked Grundfos' 80th anniversary; 21,000 colleagues delivered 5.7% sales growth in local currencies, meeting financial targets with EBIT of 10.6% of revenue.
- Customer satisfaction reached an all-time high.
- Newterra was acquired (August 2025), expanding US water treatment and reuse capabilities and strengthening position in the world's biggest pump market.
- 2025 saw 20 million additional people gain access to safely managed drinking water.
- Company remains committed to net zero in line with the Paris Agreement and supports the UN Global Compact.
- Geopolitical challenges are expected to continue into 2026.
- Key quote: "We like to say that water is the messenger of climate change."

**Financial Performance (Five-Year Overview, DKK millions)**
- Revenue 2025: DKK 34,733m (2024: 33,226); sales growth 4.5% in DKK, 5.7% in local currencies.
- EBIT before special items: DKK 3,666m (2024: 3,590); EBIT ratio 10.6% (in line with 10% strategic target).
- Profit before tax: DKK 3,770m; profit after tax: DKK 2,849m (2024: 3,433).
- Cash flow from operating activities: DKK 4,199m; free cash flow DKK 2,848m.
- Total capital investments: DKK 1,431m (4.1% of revenue); R&D cost DKK 2,206m (6.4% of revenue).
- Equity ratio: 72.0% (2024: 70.5%); return on equity 11.4%.
- Interest-bearing net deposit: DKK 6,774m; currency contracts DKK 6,630m.

**Sustainability Performance**
- Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions (market-based): 45% reduction from 2020 baseline (on track for 50% target by 2030).
- Scope 3 emissions: 25% reduction from 2020 baseline (target met for 2030).
- Total GHG emissions (scope 1, 2, 3): 106.6m t CO₂e (down from 108.3m in 2024).
- People reached with drinking water access: 20.4 million (2025) vs 17.2m (2024).
- 21,433 employees at year-end; employee motivation score 77; 40% women on Board; 25% women in leadership.
- Supplier overall CSR compliance rate: 93.4%.
- New metric: employee engagement score (3.99) will replace employee motivation from 2026.

**Strategy — Winning Aspiration 2040 & Ignite'27**
- Ignite'27 strategy launched February 2025 (2025-2027 strategic phase).
- Must-win battles: Innovate to grow, Expand through M&A, Organise for competitiveness, Win in the US.
- Four group enablers: Lead in water sustainability/net zero, Build people and organisational capabilities, Differentiate through software/digital/AI, Build efficient and resilient supply chains.
- Business model: "One Grundfos to the power of four" — four divisions (CBS, DBS, IND, WU) plus DAB and Peerless Pumps.

**Divisional Performance**
- **Commercial Building Services (CBS):** Revenue DKK 7,279m; 5% growth; strong in US and IMEA driven by data centre cooling projects; aftermarket growth strong.
- **Domestic Building Services (DBS):** Revenue DKK 7,838m; 1% growth; launched ALPHA GO range (covers ~70% of circulator pumps, up to 55% energy reduction); opened remanufacturing line in Denmark.
- **Industry (IND):** Revenue DKK 10,215m; 13% growth; integrated Newterra; double-digit growth in e-pump portfolio; strong water treatment growth.
- **Water Utility (WU):** Revenue DKK 5,144m; 5% growth; launched CUE 302 controller; growth in US, Europe, Asia and China.

**Innovation & Risk**
- 24 new products released; 98 new patents granted in 2025.
- ISO 27001 and IEC 62443 certifications for cybersecurity; completed RED Delegated Act conformity assessments.
- Export restrictions on heavy rare earth materials mitigated by earlier innovation eliminating these from permanent magnets.
- Risk management framework: Board holds ultimate responsibility; Group Management serves as risk owners.

**Outlook 2026**
- Revenue growth forecast: 4–7% in local currencies (excluding potential acquisitions/divestments).
- EBIT before special items target: 10% ratio.

**Parent Company (Grundfos Holding A/S)**
- 2,084 employees; revenue DKK 5,524m; EBIT DKK 252m; profit after tax DKK 2,846m; equity DKK 25,292m (equity ratio 79.9%).

Danfoss Strengthens Portfolio with Palladio Compressors Acquisition to Drive Sustainable Cooling Solutions in India [Danfoss](https://dk.linkedin.com/company/danfoss?trk=public_post-text) has strategically expanded its compressor portfolio with the acquisition of [Palladio Compressors Srl](https://it.linkedin.com/company/palladio-compressors?trk=public_post-text), enhancing its capabilities in screw compressor technology tailored for India’s growing demand in data centers, commercial buildings, and industrial sectors. This move supports Danfoss’ LEAP 2030 sustainability strategy by offering advanced, energy-efficient solutions using natural and low-GWP refrigerants for medium energy intensity applications. [Fabio Klein](https://dk.linkedin.com/in/fabio-klein?trk=public_post-text), Divisional President of [Danfoss Commercial Compressors S.A.](https://fr.linkedin.com/company/danfoss-commercial-compressors-s.a.?trk=public_post-text), highlighted the synergy between Danfoss and Palladio technologies, emphasizing strengthened offerings in industrial heat pumps and large-scale refrigeration. Madhur Sehgal, Head of Danfoss Climate Solutions Sales India, noted that integrating Palladio’s screw compressors enables the company to address India’s rapid urbanization and sustainability needs, supporting long-term cost competitiveness on the path to net-zero emissions. [David Candio](https://it.linkedin.com/in/davidcandio?trk=public_post-text), CEO of Palladio Compressors, welcomed the acquisition as a transformative opportunity to innovate and expand global reach while ensuring seamless customer support.   At the CII Automotive Water Conference 2025 in New Delhi, Mr. Anirban Ghosh, Co-Chairman of the Conference and Head, Centre for Sustainability, Mahindra University, reflected on how deeply water shapes both industry and livelihoods in India. He shared that even in his early career, water availability was the single biggest factor influencing the nation’s tractor sales — a reminder that economic growth and water security are inseparable. Translating that insight to manufacturing, Mr. Ghosh noted that while the automotive industry may not be as water-intensive as others, it remains highly vulnerable to water risks that can disrupt operations and supply chains. He called on the sector to reframe water investments not as compliance costs but as strategic safeguards for business continuity, urging industries to measure success by resilience as much as by efficiency. Mr. Ghosh further emphasized that the path to water security lies in collective stewardship — where industrial estates, communities, and local administrations collaborate to create shared water-positive ecosystems. # Grundfos joins forces with InPipe Energy to provide efficient, intelligent renewable energy and decarbonization technology to municipalities and industries

* November 22, 2024

**As the world works to cut greenhouse gas emissions and meet SDG-13, the imperative to limit and adapt to climate change, the new combined solution is the first product line to allow water utilities and industrial facilities to generate clean, low-cost electricity from their own water infrastructure**

**Brookshire, Texas, ****November 22, 2024**** –** [**Grundfos**](https://www.grundfos.com/us) and [**InPipe Energy (InPipe)**](https://inpipeenergy.com/), have today announced a partnership to help municipal water utilities and water-intensive industries save energy, save money and meet their climate action goals through the HydroXS® system. Within the water cycle, water distribution is the application that consumes the most energy and, unlike wastewater treatment, has no means to produce or recover resources to create energy. The HydroXS® changes this, using Grundfos pump technology as a turbine to enable users to become carbon-neutral or even carbon-positive.

Grundfos and InPipe recognized the need for efficient, intelligent renewable energy solutions that not only reduce greenhouse gas emissions and lower energy costs but also transform how water is managed.

HydroXS® is a turnkey energy recovery system that replicates the functionality of a control valve but converts typically wasted pressure in existing water pipelines into a new, low-cost source of renewable, green energy. It combines a micro-hydro turbine using Grundfos technology with smart controls so that operators can precisely manage pressure and control flow to decrease non-revenue water volumes, generate renewable energy, and reduce carbon emissions to meet sustainability, budgetary, and reliability goals. HydroXS® can be used to power critical infrastructure, or net-meter back to the grid.

*“Our collaboration with InPipe marks a significant milestone in Grundfos’ strategy to integrate pumping and technology solutions with innovative energy recovery,”* explained **Dan Story, Senior Director WU Product Management at Grundfos**. “*We’re committed to exploring innovative avenues to combat climate change alongside our customers, and InPipe’s modular approach presents a game-changing opportunity to empower our customers to enhance their operational efficiency, sustainability, and resilience.”*

*“Municipal water supply is only the beginning,”* added **InPipe CEO and Founder, Gregg Semler**.

*“Water-intensive industries like mining, food and beverage, agriculture, and data centers can also leverage their existing infrastructure investment and reduce electricity costs by recovering energy from their own water systems making the HydroXS a low-cost, drop-in solution for achieving carbon neutrality sooner than later.”*

The first HydroXS installation to incorporate Grundfos’ pump-as-a-turbine technology will be commissioned this month in Aurora, Colorado. [**Aurora Water**](https://www.auroragov.org/residents/water), providers of water, sewer, and stormwater services to City of Aurora residents, selected HydroXS as part of its plan to shift to renewable energy. It will generate an estimated 60 kilowatts of energy from the City’s water distribution system each year offsetting nearly six metric tons of CO2 emissions over its lifetime. Further project details and photos will be available in November.

### About Grundfos

Grundfos pioneers solutions to the world’s water and climate challenges to improve the quality of life for people. As a leading global pump and water solutions company, Grundfos is committed to respecting, protecting, and advancing the flow of water; by providing energy and water efficient solutions and systems for a wide range of applications for water utilities, industries, and buildings.

## Reverse Osmosis Market Outlook 2025-2034

The global **reverse osmosis market** was valued at **$8.7 billion** in 2025 and is projected to reach **$18.2 billion** by 2034, expanding at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of **8.6%** over the forecast period 2026-2034, driven by worsening global freshwater scarcity, tightening governmental water discharge regulations, and accelerating industrial and municipal water recycling mandates. Reverse osmosis technology, which uses semi-permeable membranes to remove dissolved salts, pathogens, heavy metals, and micropollutants from water streams, has become the cornerstone of modern water purification infrastructure across every major end-use sector. In 2025, water stress affects more than **3.6 billion people** worldwide, with the United Nations projecting that demand for fresh water will outpace sustainable supply by **40%** by 2030, creating a structural and irreversible growth tailwind for the reverse osmosis industry. The rapid proliferation of seawater desalination projects particularly in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries, North Africa, and coastal India is accelerating deployment of large-scale RO [desalination systems](/report/global-water-desalination-equipment-market), while simultaneous growth in pharmaceutical, semiconductor, and power generation water purity standards is driving high-specification membrane adoption in industrial segments. Membrane technology innovation, particularly in energy recovery devices and high-rejection thin-film composite membranes, is progressively reducing the specific energy consumption of RO plants from a historical average of **3.5 kWh/m3** to below **2.0 kWh/m3** in cutting-edge installations, enhancing the economic viability of RO relative to competing desalination methods. The emergence of low-pressure and ultra-low-pressure membranes for residential and light commercial applications is broadening the addressable market considerably in price-sensitive regions such as Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America. Investments in smart water infrastructure, including IoT-enabled membrane monitoring and predictive maintenance platforms, are adding a premium digital services layer to traditional hardware revenues and are expected to represent a growing proportion of total market value through 2034. Government stimulus programs, including the United States Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act allocating over **$55 billion** for water infrastructure modernization, China's 14th Five-Year Plan for water recycling, and the European Union's updated Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, are providing direct procurement impetus for RO system integrators and membrane manufacturers globally. The competitive landscape remains moderately concentrated, with the top ten players holding approximately **55-60%** of global revenue, yet increasingly challenged by regional membrane manufacturers in China, South Korea, and India offering cost-competitive alternatives to established Western brands.

## Reverse Osmosis Market Regional Outlook 2025-2034

**Asia Pacific** dominated the global reverse osmosis market in 2025, generating approximately **$3.2 billion** in revenue and commanding a **36.8%** share. The region's dominance is underpinned by severe freshwater scarcity in India, China, and Southeast Asian nations, where rapid industrial expansion and urbanization are overwhelming existing surface water and groundwater supplies. China alone accounted for a significant share of Asia Pacific RO demand in 2025, driven by its massive network of industrial parks requiring ultra-pure process water for electronics, pharmaceuticals, and textiles manufacturing, along with aggressive municipal wastewater reclamation programs targeting **80%** water reuse by 2030 under national environmental mandates. India's water sector is experiencing parallel acceleration, with central government programs such as Jal Jeevan Mission targeting piped potable water to every rural household by 2024 and subsequently requiring large-scale RO treatment investments at district water supply stations. Australia is a mature but stable RO market, with Perth's Desalination Plant and Adelaide's SA Water RO facility representing model large-scale municipal deployments that are informing similar projects across Southeast Asia. The region is projected to maintain its lead throughout the forecast period, growing at a CAGR of approximately **9.7%** through 2034, supported by government-led seawater desalination projects in coastal China, India, and Indonesia, coupled with rising per-capita income enabling residential RO penetration at a faster pace than any other region. Strategic investments by local players such as Toray Industries, LG Chem, and regional Chinese manufacturers in next-generation low-energy membranes are reinforcing Asia Pacific's competitive membrane supply chain and reducing import dependency, further stimulating domestic RO system deployments at scale.

**North America** represented the second-largest regional market in 2025, accounting for a **24.3%** share of global reverse osmosis revenues. The United States is the primary growth engine within the region, where aging municipal water infrastructure, elevated groundwater contamination from agricultural runoff and industrial discharge, and the landmark Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act are collectively catalyzing accelerated RO system procurement by utilities and municipalities. The ongoing water crisis in western U.S. states, notably California and Arizona, where prolonged droughts are depleting Colorado River allocations, is compelling water authorities to invest in large-scale water and wastewater treatment facilities incorporating RO desalination of brackish groundwater and direct potable reuse applications. The U.S. semiconductor and pharmaceutical industries, concentrated in Texas, Arizona, and the Northeast, continue to represent high-value demand centers for ultra-pure water systems, requiring multi-stage RO configurations with conductivity specifications below **0.056 microsiemens/cm**. Canada contributes a modest but growing share, with provinces such as British Columbia and Ontario investing in RO-based solutions for contaminant removal in community water systems. The North American market is expected to grow at approximately **7.8%** CAGR over 2026-2034, supported by increasing adoption of point-of-use RO purifiers in residential settings, growing awareness of lead and PFAS contamination in drinking water, and robust private sector investment in data center cooling water recycling systems.

## How does reverse osmosis compare to other water filtration technologies?

Reverse osmosis operates at the nanofiltration and below level, removing particles, dissolved salts, heavy metals, bacteria, viruses, and organic compounds with rejection rates of **95-99.9%** for total dissolved solids, far surpassing the capabilities of microfiltration (removes particles above 0.1 micrometers), ultrafiltration (removes macromolecules and colloids), and activated carbon filtration (removes organic compounds and chlorine). Unlike nanofiltration, RO effectively removes monovalent ions such as sodium and chloride, making it the only membrane technology suitable for seawater and brackish water desalination at commercial scale. However, RO operates at higher pressures (typically **5-80 bar** depending on feedwater salinity), resulting in higher energy consumption than upstream filtration technologies, which is why pre-treatment steps using coagulation, sedimentation, and macrofiltration are commonly deployed upstream to extend membrane life and reduce operational costs.

## Reverse Osmosis Market Analysis by Membrane Type

**Thin-Film Composite (TFC) Membranes** dominated the membrane type segment of the reverse osmosis market in 2025 by a substantial margin, commanding approximately **$6.3 billion** in revenue and a **72.4%** market share. TFC membranes, constructed from a thin polyamide active layer on top of a polysulfone support membrane and a polyester backing fabric, have become the industry standard for virtually all RO applications due to their superior water permeability, exceptional salt rejection rates of **99.0 to 99.7%**, and broad chemical and pH tolerance relative to earlier generation cellulose acetate membranes. The continuous innovation in TFC membrane chemistry, including the incorporation of surface modifications to impart chlorine tolerance, anti-fouling properties, and higher flux at lower operating pressures, has maintained the technology's dominant market position even as competing membrane chemistries advance. Leading TFC membrane manufacturers including Dow Water and Process Solutions (FilmTec brand), Toray Industries, Hydranautics, LG Chem, and DuPont Water Solutions (formerly Dow's membrane business) collectively control the majority of global TFC membrane production capacity, with combined annual production volumes running into billions of square meters of active membrane area. The TFC membrane segment is projected to maintain its dominance through 2034, growing at a CAGR of approximately **8.9%**, driven by replacement demand in the vast installed base of RO systems globally and by new system deployments across all geographies and end-use sectors. Nanocomposite and biomimetic variants of TFC membranes represent emerging premium sub-segments within the TFC category that are attracting significant R&D investment and are expected to command meaningfully higher unit prices than conventional polyamide TFC membranes, contributing positively to average selling price trends within the segment over the forecast period.

**Cellulose-Based Membranes** accounted for approximately **18.3%** of the reverse osmosis membrane market in 2025, representing a smaller but still commercially significant segment that retains certain application-specific advantages over TFC membranes. Cellulose triacetate (CTA) membranes in particular offer superior resistance to biological fouling and greater tolerance to free chlorine disinfectants in the feed water, making them preferred choices in certain municipal and seawater desalination applications where pre-treatment chlorination is practiced and where biological contamination of feed water is a persistent operational challenge. The Nile basin, Persian Gulf, and certain Red Sea desalination operations have historically specified CTA membranes in spiral wound modules for biofouling management reasons, and this preference persists despite the generally lower water permeability and salt rejection of cellulose membranes relative to TFC alternatives. CTA membrane demand is projected to grow at a more modest CAGR of approximately **5.8%** over 2026-2034, as TFC anti-fouling membrane formulations progressively narrow the biofouling resistance advantage of cellulose chemistry in mainstream applications. The **Others** membrane type category, covering ceramic membranes, sulfonated polyether ketone membranes, and novel nanocomposite substrate membranes, represented approximately **9.3%** of revenues in 2025 and is expected to be the fastest-growing membrane type segment, at a CAGR approaching **13.5%**, as these advanced materials transition from pilot-scale validation to commercial deployment in high-value industrial and pharmaceutical applications over the 2026-2034 forecast window. The bow water screens used upstream of RO membrane systems as primary pre-treatment for river and surface water intake protection are an important complementary technology market that tracks directionally with RO system deployments in municipal and industrial settings.

## What is the typical lifespan of a reverse osmosis membrane and system?

A well-maintained reverse osmosis membrane element typically has a service life of **3 to 7 years** in municipal and industrial applications, depending on feedwater quality, operating pressure, cleaning frequency, and system design. The overall RO system, including pressure vessels, high-pressure pumps, frames, and instrumentation, can operate for **15 to 25 years** with appropriate preventive maintenance and periodic component replacement. Advances in smart monitoring platforms introduced commercially between 2024 and 2026 use real-time flux, pressure differential, and salt passage data to predict membrane degradation **30 to 60 days** in advance, enabling planned replacement rather than emergency shutdown, which can extend effective membrane operational life by **15 to 25%** compared to traditional time-based replacement schedules.

## Reverse Osmosis Market Opportunities and Threats 2025-2034

The reverse osmosis market presents several compelling near-term and medium-term growth opportunities that industry participants are strategically positioning to capture through 2034. Direct potable reuse (DPR) represents perhaps the single largest greenfield opportunity, with regulatory frameworks for engineered direct potable reuse advancing rapidly in the United States (California, Texas, Colorado), Australia, Namibia, and Singapore, collectively representing potential new RO system demand measured in the tens of billions of dollars in capital expenditure over the next decade. The emerging green hydrogen economy constitutes a second major opportunity vector, as proton exchange membrane (PEM) and alkaline electrolysis technologies require large volumes of ultra-pure water feedstock, with global electrolyzer capacity expected to exceed **500 GW** by 2035 according to International Energy Agency projections, generating enormous incremental demand for RO-based water purification systems. In the agricultural sector, the opportunity for brackish water irrigation using RO-desalinated water in water-stressed arid and semi-arid regions is gaining credibility as energy costs for RO decline and the economic value of year-round crop production increases, with pilot programs in Israel, Spain, and the United Arab Emirates demonstrating agronomic and economic viability. Data center water recycling represents an emerging and rapidly growing commercial application, as hyperscale cloud computing and AI infrastructure operators face increasing scrutiny over their freshwater consumption for cooling and are investing in closed-loop RO-based water recycling systems to achieve water neutrality commitments. The integration of renewable solar and wind energy with RO desalination in off-grid configurations, demonstrated at commercial scale in the Canary Islands, Australia, and Chile, opens viable RO deployment pathways in remote communities and small island developing states that previously lacked affordable desalination options, representing a collectively significant incremental demand base that is cost-sensitive but not negligible in aggregate. The food waste management sector's growing focus on wastewater minimization in food processing facilities is creating parallel demand for compact RO recovery systems that can reclaim process water and reduce effluent discharge volumes and treatment costs simultaneously.

Threats to the reverse osmosis market's growth trajectory include the persistent challenge of brine disposal and concentrate management, which represents a significant environmental, regulatory, and operational hurdle for inland and coastal RO installations alike. Concentrated brine discharged from RO desalination plants into coastal marine environments can cause localized hypersalinity and ecological disruption, and multiple environmental regulatory agencies are introducing stricter concentrate disposal standards that increase project costs and complexity, potentially deterring some investment in coastal desalination capacity. The high capital and operating costs of large-scale RO systems relative to conventional water treatment alternatives remain a barrier to adoption in low-income countries and municipalities with constrained water tariff-setting authority, despite the declining cost trajectory driven by membrane improvements and energy recovery. Membrane fouling by biological slime, mineral scaling, and colloidal particles continues to impose significant operational costs and performance penalties in challenging feedwater environments, and while membrane cleaning technologies are advancing, the operational complexity of managing fouling remains a barrier to adoption among small utilities and developing-nation operators with limited technical capacity. Competition from alternative [desalination technologies](/report/global-water-desalination-equipment-market), particularly multi-effect distillation (MED) and mechanical vapor compression (MVC) in high-temperature environments where waste heat is available, and from advanced nanofiltration membranes in lower TDS removal applications, limits RO's addressable market in specific use cases. Geopolitical tensions affecting global supply chains for membrane raw materials, including polyamide and polysulfone polymers predominantly sourced from Asian and European chemical producers, introduce supply risk and cost volatility that can affect RO system manufacturer profitability and project economics. The risk of disruptive technological substitution from forward osmosis, membrane distillation, or electrochemical desalination technologies, while currently a long-range concern rather than an immediate competitive threat, warrants monitoring as R&D investments in alternative desalination approaches continue to grow across academic and commercial settings globally.

On the strategic threat side, the intensifying commoditization of standard spiral-wound RO membrane elements, driven by the rapid scale-up of Chinese membrane manufacturers such as OriginWater, Vontron, and Keensen, is compressing unit selling prices and gross margins for established Western and Japanese membrane brands in price-sensitive regional markets. Between 2020 and 2025, average selling prices for standard 4-inch and 8-inch spiral wound RO elements declined by an estimated **20-30%** in the Asia Pacific market as Chinese domestic production scaled aggressively, with similar pricing pressure beginning to manifest in Southeast Asian, African, and Latin American markets where Chinese technology exports are gaining share. This commoditization dynamic is forcing established players to differentiate increasingly on the basis of membrane performance warranties, system integration capabilities, and digital services rather than hardware specifications alone, reshaping competitive strategy across the industry and accelerating the shift toward higher-value service and solutions business models. Regulatory uncertainty in key growth markets, particularly around water tariff structures, public-private partnership frameworks, and environmental impact assessment requirements for desalination projects, can cause significant project delays and investment deferrals that temporarily dampen market growth momentum, as evidenced by the multi-year delays experienced by several major desalination projects in India and California between 2018 and 2024.

This is a market research report page from DataIntelo on the global Reverse Osmosis (RO) Market, forecast 2025-2034 (259 pages, updated April 2026, 4.9 rating, authored by Raksha Sharma, fact-checked by V. Chandola, edited by Shruti Bhat).

## Key Market Figures
- Market valued at $8.7 billion in 2025, projected to reach $18.2 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 8.6% (2026-2034).
- Thin-Film Composite (TFC) Membranes dominated membrane type with 72.4% share ($6.3B) in 2025.
- Industrial application led demand at 38.5% share ($3.35B); municipal 26.4%, residential 17.8%, commercial 11.3%.
- Asia Pacific dominated with $3.2 billion revenue and 36.8% share; North America 24.3%, Europe 20.5%, Middle East & Africa 12.1%, Latin America 6.3%.
- By product type: Desalination Systems 40.0% ($3.48B), Purification Systems 32.5%, Filtration Units 21.5%, Others 6.0%.
- By end-user: Water & Wastewater Treatment 41.9% ($3.65B), Food & Beverage 20.8%, Healthcare 14.3%, Power Generation 11.6%.
- Top ten players hold approximately 55-60% of global revenue.

## Key Growth Drivers
1. Escalating global freshwater scarcity (over 3.6 billion people affected; UN projects 40% demand-supply gap by 2030; 17 countries at extreme water stress).
2. Stringent water quality regulations (US EPA PFAS limits at 4 ppt finalized 2024; EU Drinking Water Directive 2023; China's GB 5749-2022 standard with 97 parameters).
3. Rapid industrialization and high-purity water demand (semiconductor UPW needs 18 megaohm-cm resistivity; pharmaceutical and green hydrogen sectors).
4. Technological innovation (nanocomposite TFC membranes with 3-10x permeability; energy recovery reducing RO energy from 3.5 to below 2.0 kWh/m3).

## Government Programs
- US Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act: over $55 billion for water infrastructure.
- China's 14th Five-Year Plan for water recycling (80% water reuse target by 2030).
- EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive.
- Saudi Arabia Vision 2030; UAE National Water Security Strategy 2036.
- US CHIPS and Science Act, India's Semiconductor Mission, Jal Jeevan Mission.

## Regional Dynamics
- Asia Pacific fastest growing at ~9.7% CAGR; China has 100+ million installed household RO units.
- North America growing at ~7.8% CAGR; ultra-pure water systems with conductivity below 0.056 microsiemens/cm.
- Middle East & Africa fastest regional growth at ~11.2% CAGR.
- Latin America ~8.0% CAGR.

## Technology Comparison
RO operates at nanofiltration and below level, removing TDS at 95-99.9% rejection, operating at 5-80 bar pressure. RO membrane lifespan: 3-7 years; overall system 15-25 years. Smart monitoring can extend membrane life by 15-25%.

## Market Threats
- Brine disposal and concentrate management environmental/regulatory challenges.
- High capital and operating costs in low-income regions.
- Membrane fouling issues.
- Competition from MED/MVC desalination and nanofiltration alternatives.
- Commoditization of RO membranes (Chinese manufacturers OriginWater, Vontron, Keensen driving 20-30% price declines in Asia Pacific 2020-2025).

## Competitive Landscape
Leaders: Dow Water and Process Solutions, SUEZ, Toray Industries, Hydranautics, LG Chem, Koch Membrane Systems, DuPont Water Solutions, Veolia. Second tier: Evoqua, Pentair, Axeon, Applied Membranes, Membranium, LANXESS, Toyobo, Osmoflo, IDE Technologies.

## Opportunities
Direct potable reuse, green hydrogen economy (500 GW electrolyzer capacity by 2035 per IEA), brackish water irrigation, data center water recycling, renewable-powered off-grid RO desalination.

# **DuPont™ FilmTec**™ **Nanofiltration Membranes Win 2024 Sustainability Technology of the Year**

**DuPont™ FilmTec**™ **Nanofiltration Membranes Win 2024 Sustainability Technology of the Year**

![]()
![]()
![]()
![]()

*Awarded at Global Sustainability & ESG Awards, Hosted by Sustainability LIVE*

![]()

**WILMINGTON, Del., September 17, 2024** — DuPont (NYSE:DD) today announced that FilmTec™ Nanofiltration (NF) membrane portfolio has been named the 2024 Sustainable Technology of the Year at the Global Sustainability & ESG Awards. Hosted by Sustainability LIVE, the award celebrates technologies that enable more sustainable commerce and the development of greener solutions.

Nanofiltration, a low-energy water purification membrane technology, is helping our world solve numerous goals for sustainable development — from drinking water access and industrial water reuse to lithium extraction, seawater brine recovery, and milk concentration into valuable forms of protein.

“Our team at DuPont Water Solutions is extremely proud that ourFilmTec™ Nanofiltration (NF) membrane portfolio has been named the 2024 Sustainable Technology of the Year,” said Jeroen Bloemhard, Vice President and General Manager, DuPont Water Solutions. “From supporting sustainable development goals for clean water or zero hunger, to enabling cleaner energy and climate action, the human condition is improved through the advancement and use of our nanofiltration membrane technologies.”

NF membranes are used to separate multiple solutes in a liquid feed, usually with differences in ionic charge.  In addition to water purification, this technology is used to recover, recycle, and concentrate valuable solutes in mining, industrial chemical processes, microelectronics manufacturing, dairy processing, and many more applications.

“Innovation and sustainability should not operate on parallel paths; it’s at their intersection where companies can make the biggest impact on society and solve for some of the biggest societal challenges,” said Gary Gu, Global Technology Leader, DuPont Water Solutions. “In the case of nanofiltration, DuPont’s R&D team has continuously innovated our NF products to be more durable and require less energy and support customers’ on their sustainability journey.”

DuPont offers market-leading technologies to address a variety of challenges faced by water treatment municipalities, seawater desalination plants, and industrial water users, including the microelectronics industry, through a broad portfolio of membranes, resins and complete systems. The team is also innovating solutions that help balance the world’s growing water and energy demands, with products that help maximize the availability of electricity, lithium and green hydrogen.

Technologies include reverse osmosis (RO) membranes, ion exchange resins (IEX), ultrafiltration (UF), electrodeionization (EDI), nanofiltration (NF), membrane bioreactor systems (MBR), membrane aerated biofilm reactors (MABR), and closed-circuit reverse osmosis (CCRO) systems.

**About DuPont**DuPont (NYSE: DD) is a global innovation leader with technology-based materials and solutions that help transform industries and everyday life. Our employees apply diverse science and expertise to help customers advance their best ideas and deliver essential innovations in key markets including electronics, transportation, construction, water, healthcare and worker safety. More information about the company, its businesses and solutions can be found at [www.dupont.com](https://www.dupont.com/). *Ultrafiltration, Ion Exchange, Reverse Osmosis, and Nanofiltration Now Integrated into One Advanced Water Treatment Design Platform*

WILMINGTON, Del., March 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DuPont Water Solutions today announced the expansion of Water Application Value Engine (WAVE PRO), its advanced online water treatment modeling tool, with the addition of reverse osmosis (RO) and nanofiltration (NF) capabilities. The enhanced platform now integrates ultrafiltration (UF), ion exchange (IX), RO, and NF into a single, comprehensive water treatment design solution for applications including drinking water, industrial utility water, wastewater, and seawater desalination.

WAVE PRO is the next generation of the Water Application Value Engine (WAVE) software platform, guiding water professionals through the treatment design process with a robust calculation engine that enables highly accurate system modeling. As a data‑driven software tool, WAVE PRO leverages real performance data to model complex water treatment systems. Through an intuitive digital interface, users can adjust model parameters to simulate specific feedwater conditions and operational scenarios, helping determine optimal system configurations while incorporating project specific economics to improve operating expense and water balance calculations."

"We are excited to offer our municipal and industrial customers WAVE PRO, the cloud-based latest generation of water treatment design tools—now integrating ultrafiltration, ion exchange, reverse osmosis, and nanofiltration in one comprehensive platform," said Gary Gu, Global Technology Leader, DuPont Water Solutions. "By bringing these core water treatment technologies together, WAVE PRO provides more accurate, data‑driven system design that optimizes membrane and energy use, can extend asset lifetimes, and helps customers reduce the environmental footprint of water treatment while achieving their operational and financial goals."

WAVE PRO seamlessly integrates an extensive range of DuPont Water Solutions technologies, including DuPont™ IntegraTec™ and Inge™ ultrafiltration modules, DuPont™ AmberLite™ ion exchange resins, and FilmTec™ reverse osmosis and nanofiltration elements—bringing industry‑leading filtration and separation technologies together in one powerful design environment. With the addition of reverse osmosis and nanofiltration, WAVE PRO now provides access to the FilmTec™ element portfolio for brackish water reverse osmosis membranes, seawater reverse osmosis membranes, nanofiltration elements, and FilmTec™ Fortilife™ elements, enabling more comprehensive and confident water treatment system design.

Originally launched more than a decade ago, the WAVE software platform made advanced proprietary water treatment models—refined over more than 30 years—accessible to a broader audience. Since then, WAVE has become a trusted industry tool, referenced in more than 100 technical journals and downloaded more than 16,000 times in the past three years alone. Today, WAVE PRO is utilized by more than 4,000 water treatment professionals worldwide.

Customers currently using WAVE can transition seamlessly to WAVE PRO with backward compatibility. As a web‑based platform, WAVE PRO can be accessed securely from any computer or tablet using a single sign‑in and is compatible with both Microsoft Windows and iOS. The platform supports secure collaboration and sharing across teams and automatically updates with the latest features and enhancements.

WAVE PRO is free to use and available on DuPont Water Solutions' [WaterApp](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4630987-1&h=600021562&u=https%3A%2F%2Fdupontwaterapp.com%2F&a=WaterApp), which includes a broad range of digital tools to help water professionals—from optimizing membrane cost and carbon footprint in water treatment plants, to calculating ion exchange resin replacement requirements. To directly sign in: [http://wavepro.dupont.com](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4630987-1&h=631027528&u=http%3A%2F%2Fwavepro.dupont.com%2F&a=http%3A%2F%2Fwavepro.dupont.com)

DuPont Water Solutions' technologies help purify more than 50 million gallons of water every minute in 112 countries around the world. DuPont offers a broad portfolio of membranes, resins, and complete systems to address the challenges faced by water treatment municipalities, seawater desalination plants, and industrial water users—including the microelectronics industry. The team continues to innovate solutions that support growing global water and energy demands, including technologies that enable the production of electricity, lithium, and green hydrogen.

DuPont Water Solutions announced on March 3, 2026, the expansion of its WAVE PRO (Water Application Value Engine) design tool to include reverse osmosis (RO) and nanofiltration (NF) capabilities. The platform now integrates ultrafiltration (UF), ion exchange (IX), RO, and NF into a single, comprehensive water treatment design solution for applications including drinking water, industrial utility water, wastewater, and seawater desalination.

WAVE PRO is the cloud-based next generation of the WAVE software platform, which has been a trusted industry tool referenced in more than 100 technical journals and downloaded over 16,000 times in the past three years. The enhanced platform is now used by more than 4,000 water treatment professionals worldwide.

Key features and integrations include:
- DuPont™ IntegraTec™ and Inge™ ultrafiltration modules
- DuPont™ AmberLite™ ion exchange resins
- FilmTec™ reverse osmosis and nanofiltration elements (including brackish water RO membranes, seawater RO membranes, NF elements, and FilmTec™ Fortilife™ elements)

WAVE PRO is a data-driven tool that leverages real performance data to model complex water treatment systems, allowing users to simulate specific feedwater conditions and operational scenarios, and incorporate project-specific economics to optimize operating expense and water balance calculations.

Gary Gu, Global Technology Leader at DuPont Water Solutions, stated that WAVE PRO "provides more accurate, data-driven system design that optimizes membrane and energy use, can extend asset lifetimes, and helps customers reduce the environmental footprint of water treatment while achieving their operational and financial goals."

WAVE PRO is free to use, web-based (accessible from any computer or tablet with single sign-in), compatible with both Microsoft Windows and iOS, and offers backward compatibility for existing WAVE users. It is available through DuPont's WaterApp platform or directly at wavepro.dupont.com.

DuPont Water Solutions' technologies purify more than 50 million gallons of water every minute in 112 countries. DuPont (NYSE: DD) is a global innovation leader in healthcare, water, construction, and industrial markets.
args.key_excerpts: "We are excited to offer our municipal and industrial customers WAVE PRO, the cloud-based latest generation of water treatment design tools—now integrating ultrafiltration, ion exchange, reverse osmosis, and nanofiltration in one comprehensive platform," said Gary Gu, Global Technology Leader, DuPont Water Solutions. "By bringing these core water treatment technologies together, WAVE PRO provides more accurate, data-driven system design that optimizes membrane and energy use, can extend asset lifetimes, and helps customers reduce the environmental footprint of water treatment while achieving their operational and financial goals."

This is a corrected transcript of DuPont de Nemours, Inc. (DD) Business Update Call on Water Solutions, held on March 24, 2022. The call was led by Leland Weaver, President of DuPont Water & Protection, and Christopher Mecray, Vice President of Investor Relations. The purpose was a "teach-in" to provide detailed insight into the DuPont Water Solutions business, one of three businesses within the Water & Protection (W&P) segment.

**Key Business Overview:**
- Water Solutions processes approximately 50 million gallons of water every minute globally.
- 2021 net sales of $1.4 billion.
- The business has roots going back over 70 years (Dow, Rohm and Haas lineage).
- Approximately 2,200 employees globally, with over half of revenues from the Asia Pacific region, followed by Americas and Europe.
- 2021 portfolio: ion exchange and reverse osmosis technologies comprise about 80% of the portfolio; ultrafiltration makes up the rest.

**Market Context:**
- Water scarcity affects over 40% of the global population per the UN; 2.2 billion people lack safely managed drinking water; 80% of wastewater is discharged untreated.
- By 2030, the world's population is expected to reach 8.3 billion, requiring 30% more water; demand could outstrip supply by 40%.
- By 2050, manufacturing water demands are expected to increase by 400%.

**Financial and Operational Metrics:**
- Organic compound annual sales growth of approximately 7% from 2019 through 2022, consistently growing above 2x GDP.
- Capital expenditure (CapEx) around 5% of sales (potentially rising to 5.5-6% as new capacity is brought online).
- R&D investment is 3-4% of revenues.
- Gross margins "well north of 30%."
- Sales channel breakdown: ~45% through distribution, 20-25% direct, 30-35% to OEMs/new builds.
- More than 70% of sales are replacement sales, reducing business cyclicality.
- 60% of revenue generated in emerging markets.
- Approximately 60-70 active innovation programs.

**Market Segments (estimated market sizes):**
- Industrial and desalination: ~$8 billion market
- Life sciences and specialty: ~$2 billion market
- Municipal: ~$2 billion market
- Residential and commercial: ~$1 billion market (primarily Asia Pacific)

**Technology Portfolio:**
- Core technologies: ultrafiltration (IntegraFlux, MEMCOR, inge), reverse osmosis (FilmTec), ion exchange (AmberTec, AmberLite, Duolite, Ligasep).
- Emerging technologies: closed circuit reverse osmosis (CCRO, from DesaliTec acquisition), membrane bioreactor, membrane aerated bioreactor (OxyMem acquisition), membrane contactors.
- Recent acquisitions: MEMCOR and inge (ultrafiltration), OxyMem, DesaliTec.
- Notable products: FilmTec Hypershell (heat-sanitizable RO for food/beverage), B-Free (ion exchange for reverse osmosis pretreatment).
- Global Water Technology Center in Tarragona, Spain — an industrial-scale testing and piloting facility.

**Sustainability and Partnerships:**
- Partnerships include the Water Resilience Coalition (CEO mandate signed by Ed Breen), City Water Index (sponsored with Economist Impact), and water.org.
- Many Fortune 500 companies committed to water-neutral or water-positive goals by 2030.

**Q&A Highlights:**
- Capacity constraints: most pressing constraint is in reverse osmosis (~40-45% of sales). The company is evaluating expansion of RO technology capacity, potentially greenlighting a project later in 2022 (multi-year investment).
- Addressable market: historically ~$5 billion, expanded via acquisitions; each technology (RO, IER, UF) has market share "well north of 10%." Total water addressable market including pumps, valves, disinfection is well north of $150 billion.
- Go-to-market: acquisitions (MEMCOR, DesaliTec) helped move further downstream into systems; digital system optimization seen as a growth opportunity.
- Regulatory view: Weaver stated that regulatory changes are not the primary growth driver; sustainability demand is the key driver. The company is monitoring opportunities from the $1.2 trillion US stimulus (including PFAS remediation buckets).
- Competitive position: no competitor can match the breadth and scale of DuPont's water technology portfolio.

KEY FINDINGS ON THE WATER UTILITIES INDUSTRY:

1. **Current Status**: China's water utilities industry has entered a high-quality development stage. In 2024, total national water usage was stable at 592.8 billion cubic meters. Water use per 10,000 yuan GDP and per 10,000 yuan industrial added value dropped 17.7% and 23.6% respectively versus 2020. Agricultural irrigation water efficiency coefficient rose to 0.580, urban public water supply pipeline leakage dropped below 9%, and rural tap water penetration reached 94% in 2024 (96% target achieved by 2025).

2. **Core Drivers (2026-2030)**: Policy top-level design from the "15th Five-Year Plan" focusing on water resource intensive use, ecological protection, urban-rural water integration, and smart water management; ecological civilization construction and dual-carbon goals driving green transformation; urban-rural integration and rising living standards expanding demand.

3. **Key Pain Points**: Regional imbalances in infrastructure (rural/western areas lagging), uneven digital/smart transformation (SMEs rely on traditional operations), and incomplete market-based pricing mechanisms limiting profitability. Shortage of professional talent and reliance on imported high-end equipment.

4. **Competitive Landscape**: Characterized by "state-owned enterprises leading, diversified participation, regional segmentation." Large SOE water groups dominate core businesses (urban water supply, large sewage treatment). Competition is shifting from project contracting to comprehensive competition in operations, technology, service quality, and smart capabilities. Market concentration is steadily increasing.

5. **Future Trends (2026-2030)**: Smart water utilities will achieve industry-wide penetration using big data, IoT, AI, and digital twins; water resource recycling (reclaimed water, rainwater, seawater desalination) and green low-carbon transformation will accelerate; industry focus shifts from infrastructure construction to "construction + operations + quality improvement."

6. **Recommendations**: For operators—upgrade infrastructure, accelerate digital transformation, expand into water-saving services, recycled water utilization, and water environment governance. For investors—focus on smart water technology R&D, water-saving equipment manufacturing, recycled water utilization, rural water facilities, and water ecological governance.

- A 2017-2020 survey of 194 representative water enterprises showed widespread attention and high value recognition for digital water construction.

--- SOURCE 1: Interview: digital trends in the Chinese water market | Aquatech ---
URL: https://www.aquatechtrade.com/water-stories/water-treatment/china-ai-digital-water-market-challenges-opportunties

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is an interview with Bruno Lhopiteau, managing director of Siveco China and Bluebee Tech, about digital trends in the Chinese water market. Published by Aquatech Online on Tuesday, 23 September 2025.

Key findings from the interview:

- China is among the world's fastest adopters of digital tools in the water sector, driven by government mandates like the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025). By 2024, more than 90% of urban water utilities adopted 'basic' IoT sensors for real-time monitoring. The 'Digital Water' initiative post-2020 led to Smart Water solutions in 70% of new wastewater treatment plants for predictive maintenance and leak detection. Investments exceed €10 billion annually, outpacing global averages (around 40% in Europe per IWA reports).

- Despite impressive statistics, Lhopiteau notes that many 'smart' projects did not deliver real operational outputs, with "smart money" going to non-core systems (intelligent parking, facial recognition, cosmetic SCADA upgrades) or failed IT developments.

- Intense competition characterized the market: every big water company invested heavily in IT aiming to spin off divisions and list on the stock market, while countless IoT, SCADA, GIS, and IT providers fought price wars—many did not survive. The COVID period and lack of infrastructure stimulus caused significant financing issues and restructuring, though the market is showing signs of recovery.

- Chinese firms stand out for their ability to accumulate experience quickly despite high failure rates. Investment will continue, propelling water technologies globally as Chinese firms get more involved in international projects.

- Smart water technologies (Digital Twins, 3D BIM models, IoT, BI tools) are widely adopted. Competition keeps costs relatively low. Surviving vendors will emerge as local and global players.

- Lhopiteau's French company reinvented both its technology and business model through two decades in the Chinese water market, becoming more resilient and battle-tested for global competition.

- AI use is progressing: algorithms for real-time contaminant detection claim 95% accuracy in pathogen identification; AI-powered acoustic sensors claim 85% leak detection in Beijing's network (non-revenue water losses up to 30% nationally); Beijing piloted swarm robot technology for sludge removal and pipe cleaning with efficiency gains up to 40%.

- China is the world leader in scalable IoT and big data, with projects over one million IoT devices in urban water networks (e.g., Shenzhen). AI for flood and drought management is claimed to reach accuracy levels far superior to the West.

- Three opportunity areas for international companies: 1) the Foreign Investment Encouraged Catalogue (NDRC/MOFCOM policy encouraging foreign expertise and investment in water); 2) the Belt and Road Initiative opening avenues for business with Chinese firms in overseas projects (Southeast Asia, Africa); 3) rural water infrastructure with multilateral agency funding (e.g., World Bank), though Lowest-Priced Technically Acceptable tenders favor local players.

- China lags in interoperability and standardisation (data silos, slow ISO 50001 adoption), though Lhopiteau views this as temporary, citing China's early involvement in designing ISO 55000 (national standard GB/T 33172) and its capacity for fast standardisation demonstrated in power generation.

- The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), currently in drafting, emphasizes AI for 'new quality productive forces' in water with indications of €50+ billion investment for 'water security' amid climate risks. Likely outcomes include AI mandates, potential calls for increased international firm involvement in PPP projects (currently only Suez, Veolia, and Sembcorp remain as foreign water players in China), continued priorities on rural infrastructure and cutting water losses, and water tech exports via Belt and Road.

The article also promotes Aquatech China, the leading water technology trade show in China, running November 5-7 in Shanghai.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Adoption accelerated post-2020 with the 'Digital Water' initiative, with Smart Water solutions deployed in 70 per cent of new wastewater treatment plants for predictive maintenance and leak detection." - Lhopiteau
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: High Fidelity Digital Twin: Enhancing Water Management in Singapore ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xuDiXaBIFZs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video from Bentley Systems highlights PUB, Singapore's National Water Agency, being awarded the Founders' Honors for their project "High Fidelity Digital Twin-Enabled Anomaly Detection and Localization in Singapore." The project addresses the challenge of underground water leaks—in 2022, Singapore experienced an average of 4.1 reported water leaks per 100km of pipe, most of which were underground and hidden. PUB deployed hundreds of monitoring stations across the city's underground water pipes as part of its Smart Water Grid (SWG) initiative, creating a live digital twin of the water network using real-time sensor updates maintained around the clock. Engineers then applied machine learning to the sensor data to refine predictive analysis models and continuously update them, enabling the modeling and prediction of flows and pressures, tracking the health status of different zones, and continuously recalibrating and retraining the digital twin. This capability, called the Anomaly Leak Finder (ALF), detects anomalies—especially hidden leaks and pipe bursts—and locates them for field crews. ALF was benchmarked with historical data to validate its effectiveness, and in 2024 it detected two operational leaks that were verified by field crews. The major economic gain for PUB is reduced time spent on manual inspections (which are time-consuming and ineffective for hidden underground leaks), replaced by monitoring the water network through the live digital twin constantly updated by sensor data.

--- SOURCE 6: High Fidelity Digital Twin: Enhancing Water Management in ... ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xuDiXaBIFZs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video from Bentley Systems highlights PUB, Singapore's National Water Agency, being awarded the Founders' Honors for their project "High Fidelity Digital Twin-Enabled Anomaly Detection and Localization in Singapore." The project addresses the challenge of underground water leaks—in 2022, Singapore experienced an average of 4.1 reported water leaks per 100km of pipe, most of which were underground and hidden. PUB deployed hundreds of monitoring stations across the city's underground water pipes as part of its Smart Water Grid (SWG) initiative, creating a live digital twin of the water network using real-time sensor updates maintained around the clock. Engineers then applied machine learning to the sensor data to refine predictive analysis models and continuously update them, enabling the modeling and prediction of flows and pressures, tracking the health status of different zones, and continuously recalibrating and retraining the digital twin. This capability, called the Anomaly Leak Finder (ALF), detects anomalies—especially hidden leaks and pipe bursts—and locates them for field crews. ALF was benchmarked with historical data to validate its effectiveness, and in 2024 it detected two operational leaks that were verified by field crews. The major economic gain for PUB is reduced time spent on manual inspections (which are time-consuming and ineffective for hidden underground leaks), replaced by monitoring the water network through the live digital twin constantly updated by sensor data.
</summary>
